rows.why_this_matters: A street can preserve a route while its name changes. This marker helps readers see Indigenous travel, colonial landholding, and the development of public roads as connected parts of Seaford’s history.

rows.title: Islip: Colonial Estates and Continuing Native Rights
rows.summary: William Nicoll’s 1683 agreement retained Native residence, planting and fishing rights on land he had not developed. English patents strengthened private estate claims, but Native residents remained. Islip’s separate estates show why a deed, a colonial patent and a town are different parts of land-loss history.
rows.address_label: West Islip to Bayport mainland — regional historical context
rows.why_this_matters: The English deed itself retained Native rights, while later patents strengthened a private estate. Reading those records alongside evidence of Native residents in 1798 challenges the idea that paper ownership meant people or their relationships with the land had vanished.

rows.title: Jabash
rows.summary: Jabash is a Shinnecock Neck placename recorded by William Wallace Tooker for a cove on the east side of the neck. one Native resident on the neck called it Irabash cove.
rows.address_label: East side of Shinnecock Neck, Southampton, NY (approximate)

rows.title: Jamaica
rows.summary: Jamaica is a Queens placename preserved through early town and purchase records.
rows.address_label: Jamaica / Beaver Pond vicinity, Queens, NY (approximate)

rows.title: Jamaica: Native Agreements and an Expanding Colonial Town
rows.summary: Named Native agreements, settler farm allocations and later colonial patents reshaped southern Queens. Jamaica’s land claims expanded over decades; the 1655 deed did not transfer the entire later town or erase Native people.
rows.address_label: Jamaica and Queens-side bay islands — regional historical context
rows.why_this_matters: A deed date alone hides the people, unequal power and consequences involved. Read the promises and removal demands alongside Native perspectives and continuing Lenape presence.

rows.title: Jamesport Site
rows.summary: The Jamesport Site is an Orient Period (1,000-1,300 BC) ceremonial burial ground. Archaeological work documented red ochre, burial offerings, and deliberately broken stone vessels associated with ceremonial practice. Riverhead Town purchased the land in 2017 because of its cultural significance and the need for protection.
rows.activity_update_summary: Consolidated dated history into the cited Historic Timeline so the listing no longer repeats the same content.

rows.title: Jason's Rock
rows.summary: Jason's Rock is a large glacial boulder in Northwest Woods remembered through stories of a Montaukett traveler named Jason who paused there on journeys between East Hampton and Sag Harbor. The place connects Native movement, rest, water, and memory in the local landscape.

rows.title: Jones Beach Drift Whale Rights
rows.summary: Tackapousha and Native communities asserted rights to valuable marine resources, including drift whales along the south shore barrier beaches. The modern Jones Beach landscape is therefore also a place to discuss Native jurisdiction, marine economies, and colonial legal change.
rows.address_label: Jones Beach barrier beach landscape, Jones Inlet vicinity
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Linked to Merrick Ancestral Land as part of the south shore/barrier beach history; also connected with Massapequa leadership and overlapping regional authority.
rows.why_this_matters: Jones Beach is usually remembered as a modern public beach, but older records connect the barrier island to Native marine rights and coastal economies. The site carries histories of Indigenous jurisdiction and resource knowledge within a familiar public landscape.

rows.title: Kantuck
rows.summary: Kantuck is recorded as a locality in Oyster Bay, historically in Queens County and now in Nassau County. The place is described as wild, hilly, and swampy land at the head of a broad salt meadow.
rows.address_label: Beaver Swamp Creek / Mill Neck, Oyster Bay, NY (approximate)

rows.title: Kanungum / Conungum
rows.summary: Kanungum, also written Conungum or Conungam, names a pond widening the Peconic River at Calverton in Tooker’s account of Southampton’s northwestern boundary.
rows.address_label: Calverton, Riverhead, NY (approximate)

rows.title: Keemiscomock
rows.summary: Keemiscomock is recorded by William Wallace Tooker as a small brook dividing the shores of Saghtekoos, also known as Apple Tree Neck, in Islip. The same brook was also called Weepoose.
rows.address_label: Sagtikos / Apple Tree Neck, Islip, NY (approximate)

rows.title: Keskaechqueren
rows.summary: Keskaechqueren, also recorded as Keskaechquerem, was a Canarsie village near Flatlands in Brooklyn and is interpreted through language for a gathering place.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Canarsie Traditional Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Ketanomocke
rows.summary: Ketanomocke, also written Ketewamoke and Ketan-om-muck, is associated with Huntington and interpreted as a shoreline or beach placename.
rows.address_label: General Huntington / East Northport area, Suffolk County, New York

rows.title: Ketchaponack
rows.summary: Ketchaponack is a Southampton placename for a neck of land in the Westhampton Beach area, in the western part of Southampton town on Quantuck Creek near the historic West Hampton post office area.
rows.address_label: General Ketchaponack / Quantuck Creek area, Westhampton Beach, New York

rows.title: Ketumpscut / Catumb Reef
rows.summary: Ketumpscut is a Fishers Island-area placename connected with Catumb Reef, now identified as Catumb Rocks in the reef complex east of Fishers Island. Catumb and Ketumpscut are cross-referenced names for the same rocky offshore place.
rows.address_label: Catumb Rocks / Catumb Reef, reef complex east of Fishers Island between Sugar Reef and Lords Passage

rows.title: Killis
rows.summary: Killis is a Bridgehampton pond placename that survives in the modern Kellis Pond name. The pond is recorded, and its name is connected with a Native person who lived near the water, while also noting later spellings and family-name forms.
rows.address_label: Kellis Pond, Bridgehampton, New York

rows.title: Kioshk / Ellis Island
rows.summary: Kioshk is the recorded name for Ellis Island in New York Harbor. The source record is careful that this was not presented as an older local deed name; Henry R. Schoolcraft applied the Chippewa-derived name to the island in 1845.
rows.address_label: Ellis Island, New York Harbor

rows.title: Kissena Pond
rows.summary: Kissena is the recorded name for a pond at Flushing in Queens. The source immediately cautions that it is not an original Long Island name, but a later name applied to a body of water now associated with Kissena Park.
rows.address_label: Kissena Lake / Kissena Park, Flushing, Queens, New York

rows.title: Kitchaminchok
rows.summary: A Moriches Island boundary placename appearing in seventeenth-century whaling and estate records, with related forms including Ketchininchoge and Cochiminchoake.
rows.address_label: Moriches Island, Moriches Bay, East Moriches, NY (approximate)

rows.title: Konkhunganik
rows.summary: Konkhunganik is the recorded name for the southern part of Fort Pond at Montauk. In the deed language he cites, Fort Pond is described with Quanuntowunk on the north and Konkhunganik on the south.
rows.address_label: Southern Fort Pond, Montauk, NY (broad water orientation)

rows.title: Lake Agawam
rows.summary: Lake Agawam is the modern Southampton pond connected with the Agawom or Agawam entry. The broader application of Agawam to Southampton is presented as a historical error rather than a secure local Indigenous placename. The more specific place is the town pond in Southampton Village, while earlier writers mistakenly applied Agawam to the whole town.
rows.address_label: Lake Agawam, Southampton Village, NY

rows.title: Little Caughnawaga — Mohawk Brooklyn
rows.summary: From the 1920s to the 1960s, Mohawk ironworkers from Kahnawake and their families made Boerum Hill their home. Known as Little Caughnawaga, it was the largest Mohawk community outside Canada, and its men helped raise New York’s bridges and skyscrapers.
rows.address_label: Pacific Street at Nevins Street, Boerum Hill, Brooklyn, NY
rows.why_this_matters: Native Brooklyn did not end in the 1600s. In the twentieth century, Mohawk families built a community here while their work raised the city’s skyline.

rows.title: Little Church
rows.summary: Around 1844, the “ Little Church ” is built on the reservation. It was a Millerite Church, a branch of the 7th day Adventist Congregationalist church. The Millerites were part of the great revival from upstate NY. Today, there is little evidence of the church beyond photographs.
rows.activity_update_summary: Consolidated the existing dated chronology into cited Historic Moments and removed the duplicate unformatted history block.

rows.title: Long Island Museum
rows.summary: Enduring Heart brings Native history and contemporary art to Stony Brook, August 20–December 20, 2026. Explore the museum’s connections to Shinnecock decoy carving, Native storytelling, and living cultural traditions.
rows.address_label: 1200 Route 25A, Stony Brook, NY 11790
rows.why_this_matters: The story of a decoy changes when its maker is named. Research on the Herrick decoys connects museum objects with Shinnecock artist Charles Sumner Bunn, while Enduring Heart gives contemporary Native artists room to tell their own stories. Together, these histories invite visitors to look at both the object and the person whose knowledge shaped it.

rows.title: Lusam / Lusum (Jericho)
rows.summary: Lusam is a recorded older name for Jericho. Its inclusion on Indigenous place-name maps deserves context: Tooker questioned whether the name was Indigenous at all.
rows.address_label: Present-day Jericho, NY — public orientation point at Jericho Public Library
rows.why_this_matters: Not every unfamiliar historical name is necessarily Indigenous. Keeping the evidence and the uncertainty together helps prevent an old attribution from becoming an unquestioned fact.

rows.title: Ma's House
rows.summary: Ma's House & BIPOC Art Studio is a Native-led arts organization and community space on the Shinnecock Indian Reservation. Founded by Shinnecock artist and photographer Jeremy Dennis, the project began in June 2020 and became a New York nonprofit in 2021. The family house supports artist residencies, exhibitions, a shared studio and library, and art and history programs for the Shinnecock community and visiting artists.
rows.address_label: 159 Old Point Road, Southampton, NY 11969
rows.activity_update_summary: Added respectful visiting guidance with a concise answer, context, and source references.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: On Shinnecock ancestral land / Shinnecock Indian Reservation.

rows.title: Macutteris
rows.summary: Macutteris is a Flatlands placename identified from a May 13, 1664 deed for upland and marshes in what is now Brooklyn. It appears in the same deed context as Hoopaninak and Shanscomacocke.
rows.address_label: General Flatlands / Jamaica Bay marsh area, Brooklyn, New York

rows.title: Madnans / Madnank
rows.summary: Madnans or Madnank carries an uncertain Great Neck place-name history, with a possible hilly-place interpretation in older records.
rows.address_label: General Great Neck peninsula, North Hempstead, New York

rows.title: Mahchongitchuge
rows.summary: Mahchongitchuge is a Montauk North Neck swamp name recorded from the 1670 deed for the land between the ponds. The deed places it in a boundary sequence running through the swamp toward Great Pond.
rows.address_label: General North Neck swamp area between Fort Pond and Great Pond / Lake Montauk

rows.title: Makeopaca
rows.summary: Makeopaca is a Gravesend placename from a July 1684 land transfer, with Moeung marking the eastward end of the beach in the boundary description.
rows.address_label: General Gravesend / Strome Kill area, Brooklyn, New York

rows.title: Mamanock Neck
rows.summary: Mamanock names a neck of land at East Moriches in Brookhaven. The cited records place Mamanock with Meritces, or Moriches Neck, suggesting a connected pair of necks along the south shore.
rows.address_label: General Mamanock Neck / East Moriches shoreline, New York

rows.title: Manantic / Menantic Creek
rows.summary: Manantic names a neck and creek in the western part of Shelter Island. The same source notes that Shelter Island people pronounced and spelled the name locally as Menantic.
rows.address_label: General Menantic Creek / Menantic Neck area, Shelter Island, New York

rows.title: Manchonack / Gardiners Island
rows.summary: Manchonack is Tooker's placename for Gardiners Island in East Hampton. The name appears in the 1639 deed by Yovawan, sachem of Pommanocc, and Aswaw to Lion Gardiner. The name is interpreted as a land of the departed.
rows.address_label: Gardiners Island, East Hampton, New York

rows.title: Manetuck
rows.summary: An Islip neck name connected with the 1701 Watchogue sale and an interpretation as a pine or cedar swamp.
rows.address_label: General West Bay Shore / Islip neck area, New York

rows.title: Manhansack-aqua-quash-awamock
rows.summary: Manhansack-aqua-quash-awamock is a Shelter Island placename associated with Manhanset history and seventeenth-century records. The map shades the whole island because the name belongs to it broadly, not to an exact historic boundary.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Manhansett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Manhansett Ancestral Land
rows.summary: Shelter Island is Manhansett ancestral land, known in historical records as Manhansack-Ahaquatuwamock. Its waters connected Native communities long before a colonial plantation occupied the island. Land loss and plantation labor reshaped life here without making Native people simply disappear. Manhansett history includes documented political and cultural relationships with Montauk people; honoring it means remembering those connections as well as the ancestry beneath today’s island landscape.
rows.why_this_matters: Manhansett Ancestral Land presents Shelter Island as Native homeland with its own language, records, and community memory. Broad territory pages need care when related places include sensitive burial and descendant histories.

rows.title: Manhansuck (Pipe's Neck Creek)
rows.summary: Manhansuck is a Southold placename for Pipe's Neck Creek, just west of Greenport. The name belongs to a creek and outlet setting near Pipe's Cove.
rows.address_label: Pipe's Cove / Pipe's Neck Creek, west of Greenport

rows.title: Manhasset
rows.summary: Manhasset names the village and neck formerly called Cow Neck in present-day Nassau County.
rows.address_label: Manhasset, Nassau County

rows.title: Manhattan
rows.summary: Manhattan is included among Long Island and adjacent island Native place names. Because Manhattan sits in Lenape/Munsee language territory, the name should not be flattened into a generic Algonquian label. The blue marker orients readers to the modern island, not an exact historic site.
rows.address_label: Manhattan Island, New York City
rows.why_this_matters: Manhattan preserves an Indigenous name at the center of one of the world's most familiar cityscapes. Later printed spellings and translations are partial evidence rather than final meanings. The name continues to point toward Lenape presence, language, and relationships with this island.

rows.title: Manitou Hill
rows.summary: Manitou Hill, also recorded as Mannatto, is the Manetto Hill ridge area in Plainview/Oyster Bay. The placename is connected with a 1695 deed and interpreted through the Manitto, or Great Spirit, tradition.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Matinecock Traditional Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Manittuwond / Plum Island
rows.summary: An eastern island place name connected with older Indigenous fishing and planting memory around the Long Island Sound and Pequot region.
rows.address_label: Plum Island, Town of Southold

rows.title: Mannahanning / Coney Island
rows.summary: A Coney Island name from Kings County, shown as a modern orientation point rather than an exact 1654 deed boundary.
rows.address_label: Coney Island, Brooklyn
rows.why_this_matters: Before it was a resort, Coney Island was Mannahanning, “island land,” and a named Native holder, Guttaquoh, released his rights to it in 1654.

rows.title: Manor of St. George
rows.summary: Established in 1696 by Colonel William Tangier Smith, the Manor of St. George sits on Unkechaug homelands and is deeply tied to the early colonial economy of Long Island. Smith documented labor transactions with Unkechaug Native whalers and workers in The Pigskin Book (1696–1721), a record that reveals how Indigenous labor and maritime knowledge sustained coastal industries during a period of near-shore whaling carried out in small cedar boats. After Smith’s death, the ledger continued with indenture agreements.
rows.activity_update_summary: Consolidated dated history into the cited Historic Timeline so the listing no longer repeats the same content.

rows.title: Manowtassquot / Namkee Creek
rows.summary: Manowtassquot and Namkee name creek-boundary geography west of Blue Point. The Namkee entry connects the creek mouth with fishing-place language and a remembered fishing-weir setting.
rows.address_label: Namkee Creek west of Blue Point, NY (approximate waterway orientation)

rows.title: Mantoobaugs
rows.summary: Mantoobaugs is Tooker's name for a reserved parcel on Hashamomuk Neck in Southold, associated with swamps, corn fields, and the Five Wigwams area. The blue marker is approximate.
rows.address_label: General Hashamomuk Neck / Arshamomaque area near Greenport

rows.title: Manunkquiaug
rows.summary: Manunkquiaug is a Montauk placename in the North Neck area, near Great Pond, now Lake Montauk. It appears as a boundary point in a 1670 Montauk deed.
rows.address_label: General eastern/southern Great Pond (Lake Montauk) boundary area

rows.title: Marechkawick
rows.summary: Marechkawick names a Native village associated with the site of Brooklyn in early Dutch colonial records. Recorded spellings include Marychkenwikingh, Merechkawick, Merchkawikingh, and Rechkewick. Reckkewick is a cross-reference form associated with the same Brooklyn landscape.
rows.why_this_matters: Marechkawieck’s corn fields fed a Lenape town at the heart of today’s Brooklyn, and their seizure in 1643 helped ignite war across western Long Island.

rows.title: Marratooka
rows.summary: Marratooka is a Mattituck placename for a pond and the farm bordering it in Southold town. The history gives Marritook as a related form and treats Marratooka as a later form connected with Mattituck.

rows.title: Mashashimuet
rows.summary: Mashashimuet names the springs on the south side of Otter Pond in Sag Harbor. The place is associated with today's Mashashimuet Park and Otter Pond landscape, and the name was remembered through Montaukett and local Native knowledge shared with William Wallace Tooker.

rows.title: Mashmanock
rows.summary: Mashmanock is a Southampton placename connected with Canoe Place Creek near the Canoe Place isthmus and Shinnecock Canal. The name is also cross-referenced to Mashomuck, and a later Toyonge entry creates a location question by associating the 1648 deed reference with Red Creek.

rows.title: Mashomuck
rows.summary: Mashomuck is a Shelter Island placename for the southern neck and point opposite Sag Harbor, now associated with Mashomack Preserve. Recorded forms include Meshomac, Marshammock, Mashomuk, Mashomuck, and the local pronunciation Mashom-uk.

rows.title: Maskachoung / Maskutchoung
rows.summary: Maskachoung, also written Maskutchoung, is recorded as a Native placename associated with a neck of land on the southern part of the Hempstead Plains. Strong discusses George Weeks's listing of Maskutchoung as a Native community near Hempstead. The name is interpreted as a grassland or prairie place.
rows.address_label: Southern Hempstead Plains / East Meadow area
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Linked to Merrick Ancestral Land as an interior Hempstead Plains placename and Native community reference near the south shore homeland.
rows.why_this_matters: Maskachoung shows that Merrick ancestral land was not only shoreline and bay. The Hempstead Plains were also Native geography, remembered through names for grassland, prairie, community, and movement between the interior and the south shore.

rows.title: Maspeth / Mespaetches
rows.summary: Maspeth, recorded in older forms such as Mespaetches, is a Queens placename tied to Newtown Creek and its former swamp landscape.

rows.title: Massabarkem (Gravesend Neck)
rows.summary: Massabarkem is a Gravesend Neck placename in Kings County, connected with a 1650 confirmatory deed and related forms later discussed as Maseebackhun or Massebackhun.

rows.title: Massakack (Half Hollow Hills)
rows.summary: A Huntington hills placename, also written Massaback, translated as great hill land.

rows.title: Massapeoque Meadows / South Oyster Bay
rows.summary: The Massapeoque meadow landscape connects Massapequa history with the tidal waters of South Oyster Bay. Native place names, coastal livelihoods, and later land claims reveal how wetlands could be both a home landscape and a contested resource.
rows.address_label: South Oyster Bay marsh and meadow landscape, Massapequa-Seaford area
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Linked to Merrick Ancestral Land with note that Massapequa and Merrick histories overlap across the south shore.
rows.why_this_matters: Massapeoque Meadows presents wetlands as Indigenous homelands and working landscapes. Salt meadows supported hunting, fishing, shellfishing, travel, and later colonial claims over land and resources.

rows.title: Massapequa Ancestral Lands
rows.summary: Massapequa’s name connects today’s community to an older Native homeland around South Oyster Bay and Fort Neck. Leaders such as Tackapousha defended Native interests as colonial settlement pressed into fields, meadows and waterways. Those histories were connected to neighboring peoples through diplomacy and shared claims. Remembering Massapequa honors that ancestry: losing land, or a separate tribal name, did not mean its people disappeared.
rows.why_this_matters: Massapequa Ancestral Lands centers South Oyster Bay and Fort Neck as Native homeland and a place of diplomacy, defense, waterways, and land struggle. Massapequa, Merrick, Secatogue, Rockaway, and neighboring histories are often connected through these waters, records, and relationships.

rows.title: Massapequas
rows.summary: Massapequas connects Massapequa territory with south shore shell-heap and homeland context. Its place on the map is approximate, to protect burial grounds, archaeological sites and private homes.
rows.address_label: Massapequa south shore territory, Nassau County, New York (approximate public area)

rows.title: Massapootupaug
rows.summary: Massapootupaug is a western Southampton placename connected with a 1662 Shinnecock conveyance boundary near Niamack, Canoe Place, and the old gutt.

rows.title: Massepe (Thurston's Creek)
rows.summary: Massepe is a Jamaica, Queens placename for a river or creek, probably the waterway later known as Thurston's Creek or Thurston Basin.

rows.title: Mastic
rows.summary: Mastic is a Brookhaven placename associated with the Mastic Peninsula and especially the Forge River, interpreted as a great river or great tidal river.
rows.address_label: General Forge River / Mastic Peninsula area, Brookhaven, NY

rows.title: Matanucke (Staten Island)
rows.summary: This Staten Island entry gathers related names discussed in Tooker, including Matanucke, Monocknong, and Aquehonga Manacknong. Monocknong is treated here as a cross-reference variant, not as a separate mapped site.

rows.title: Matinecock Town Hall Confrontation
rows.summary: In 1969, Princess Sun Tama (Ann Harding Murdock), Lee Canevari, Janet Hannani, and the Matinecock Indian Council confronted Huntington officials over Matinecock land claims and recognition. They challenged the town's reliance on colonial deeds and insisted that Matinecock title, memory, and political identity did not depend on whether officials acknowledged it.
rows.address_label: Huntington Town Hall, Huntington
rows.why_this_matters: This stop shows municipal confrontation as a form of Native political action and land-claim advocacy.

rows.title: Matinecock Traditional Land
rows.summary: Matinecock ancestral land reaches across the North Shore from Queens into Long Island. Its people remain present through descendant families, community history and cultural work, including documented kinship with Montaukett families. Land loss and even the removal of ancestors from a burial ground did not erase that belonging. Matinecock place names and family histories ask us to recognize a living community, not a people confined to the past.
rows.why_this_matters: Matinecock Traditional Land presents the North Shore as Native geography shaped by hills, harbors, observation places, travel, diplomacy, and continuing community memory.

rows.title: Matinecock Tribal Nation
rows.summary: The Matinecock Nation, an Algonquian people, has been the steward of northwestern Long Island since time immemorial. Their name, meaning “at the hilly land,” reflects an ancestral relationship with a territory extending along the North Shore from Flushing Bay to the Nissequogue River in present-day Smithtown. Long before European contact, Matinecock ancestors lived in extensive villages at Flushing, Port Washington, Glen Cove, Oyster Bay, Cold Spring Harbor, Huntington, and Northport, where numerous village sites.
rows.activity_update_summary: Consolidated the existing dated chronology into cited Historic Moments and removed the duplicate unformatted history block.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Matinecock Traditional Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Matinecock Way
rows.summary: Matinecock Way is the co-name adopted in 2015 for the intersection of Northern Boulevard and Marathon Parkway in Little Neck. The name honors the Matinecock, who are still here, and the Native history of northeastern Queens, which is not only in the past.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Matinecock Traditional Land on the current ancestral territory map.
rows.why_this_matters: Matinecock Way places a Native community name in the everyday geography of Little Neck. Matinecock people were present at the 2015 unveiling, and the co-name recognizes that their relationship to Queens and Long Island continues.

rows.title: Matowcas (Brooklyn)
rows.summary: Matowcas is a Brooklyn-area placename and broader territory name connected with the Native sachemdom associated with what became Brooklyn.

rows.title: Mattawommax (Probable Fireplace Meadow)
rows.summary: Mattawommax named a meadow locality in Brookhaven. Brookhaven's early town records place John Thompson's numbered meadow share in the 1664 Old Purchase at South, the landscape now associated with Brookhaven Hamlet, Bellport, and Fireplace Neck; the marker is a broad probable placement rather than an identified lot boundary.
rows.address_label: Fireplace Neck, Brookhaven, NY (probable broad landscape)
rows.why_this_matters: Mattawommax preserves a Native name within the salt-meadow geography that drew Setauket proprietors to Brookhaven's south shore. Linking the deed to the Old Purchase at South makes the record visible while the probable label keeps a numbered colonial share from being mistaken for an exact recovered Native boundary.

rows.title: Mattemoy (Mastic Neck)
rows.summary: William Wallace Tooker links Mattemoy with one of the smaller necks of Mastic in Brookhaven. The name also appears as Mottemog in Long Island historical writing.

rows.title: Matthabanks (Great South Beach)
rows.summary: Matthabanks is a placename for the Great South Beach opposite Brookhaven, on the barrier island now generally known as Fire Island.

rows.title: Mattituck
rows.summary: Mattituck is the name of a village, bay, and creek in Southold. The placename remains attached to a living North Fork hamlet and its surrounding waterways.

rows.title: Mattock (North Sea Swamp)
rows.summary: Mattock is connected with a swamp near North Sea in Southampton. The name appears in eighteenth-century local records and may preserve either a description of swampy land or a personal name.

rows.title: Mattuck Brook (East Moriches)
rows.summary: Mattuck is a recorded East Moriches brook name used as the eastern boundary of Watchogue Neck. Tooker's 1911 interpretation—“bad creek”—is explicitly uncertain, and the surrounding records also preserve a 1679 land purchase and Mayhue's 1680 reference to his kinsman Warishone living west of Watchogue.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added a cited introduction connecting the Mattuck brook name to Watchogue's recorded boundaries, Tooker's uncertain interpretation, the 1677–1679 purchase record, and Mayhue's 1680 reference to his kinsman Warishone; corrected the displayed source pages and linked the existing Historic Moments.
rows.why_this_matters: Mattuck is more than a proposed translation. The name connects a brook, neighboring waterways, a land purchase, and the home of Mayhue's kinsman Warishone, remembered in a 1680 deed. Reading those records together keeps kinship and residence visible while making clear that colonial boundary descriptions do not identify an exact modern watercourse or provide a complete Native account of the land.

rows.title: Mechawanienck (New Utrecht)
rows.summary: Mechawanienck is a locality in Kings County. The name appears in a New Utrecht deed describing land running from Gouwanis across the hills toward the southeast side of Amersfoort, or Flatlands.
rows.why_this_matters: The name may preserve a Lenape route across Brooklyn’s hills that was already old when the 1652 deed was written.

rows.title: Mechowodt Treaty and Reserved Rights Landscape, 1639
rows.summary: A 1639 Dutch agreement associated with Mechowodt of the Massapequa/Marossepinck world describes Native people reserving rights to remain on the land, plant corn, fish, hunt, and make a living there.
rows.address_label: South shore landscape, Rockaway-to-Suffolk treaty context
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Linked to Merrick Ancestral Land as part of a broader south shore diplomatic and land-rights context involving overlapping Native polities.
rows.why_this_matters: The Mechowodt agreement complicates simple stories of land "sale." It shows Native leaders negotiating continued use and presence, and it helps explain how colonial legal records could both preserve Native claims and become instruments of dispossession.

rows.title: Mecox (Bridgehampton)
rows.summary: Meacox is connected with a farming district and inland bay at Bridgehampton. The modern spelling Mecox remains attached to Mecox Bay and the surrounding Bridgehampton landscape.

rows.title: Meitowax (Long Island)
rows.summary: Meitowax is a Long Island-wide name connected with map, patent, and historical variants including Matouwac, Metoac, Matowcas, Mattanwake, and Matowa.

rows.title: Memanusack (Stony Brook)
rows.summary: Memanusack, also recorded as Memanusuck, is connected with the stream from which Stony Brook takes its name. The waterway is described as an outlet from a pond into the harbor.
rows.address_label: Stony Brook Grist Mill pond outlet, Stony Brook, NY (broad waterway orientation)

rows.title: Meroke Preserve: A Name in the Wetlands
rows.summary: Meroke Preserve carries a Native regional name into a protected wetland landscape along Newbridge Creek in Bellmore.
rows.address_label: Meroke Preserve, Orange and Farmer streets, Bellmore
rows.listing_image_alt: Wooded trail at Meroke Preserve. Photograph © Jeremy Dennis, September 12, 2026.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: The preserve carries a historical form of the Merrick name.
rows.why_this_matters: Meroke remains part of the everyday geography of the South Shore. Connecting the name with a protected creek landscape invites people to learn its history while caring for the place that now carries it.

rows.title: Merrick (Hempstead Plains)
rows.summary: Merrick is a Hempstead-area placename connected with the great plain south of Hempstead and later Merrick community names.

rows.title: Merrick Ancestral Land
rows.summary: Merrick’s name recalls the Merikoke homeland of plains, creeks and South Shore waters. Native leaders challenged colonial claims here, including an unpaid-land dispute in 1675; later records still describe Native community life. The name’s survival should prompt more than remembrance of a vanished past. Native people continue to gather and assert belonging on this coast, while the histories of particular Merrick families deserve careful, descendant-informed attention.
rows.address_label: Broad Merrick / Freeport / Bellmore / Hempstead Plains and south shore wetland landscape, Nassau County, NY
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Primary Merrick ancestral land record for related south shore and Hempstead Plains related south shore and Hempstead Plains entries.
rows.why_this_matters: Merrick Ancestral Land presents Nassau County's south shore as Native homeland: a place of language, plains, creeks, shellfish waters, travel routes, diplomacy, and continuing memory. The Merrick/Meroke references also shows that colonial land loss was contested. Native leaders and communities remained active in negotiations, legal challenges, kinship networks, and public memory long after early deeds were written.

rows.title: Merrick Community in Horton’s Journal, 1742
rows.summary: Azariah Horton’s June 7, 1742 journal entry records a visit to Native people at Merrick during his travels along Long Island’s South Shore.
rows.address_label: Merrick community; meeting place not identified
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Linked to Merrick Ancestral Land as eighteenth-century evidence of Native presence in the Merrick area.
rows.why_this_matters: Horton’s journal records Native people living in Merrick long after colonial land transactions. Their presence is part of a continuing community history that accounts of settlement often overlook.

rows.title: Merrick Homeland and Historical Boundary Maps
rows.summary: Native communities on western Long Island were connected through neighboring villages, kinship, and shared landscapes.
rows.address_label: Merrick regional history; no identified western-boundary site
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Merrick history includes relationships with neighboring Native communities across western Long Island.
rows.why_this_matters: Maps can make connected communities appear separate. The histories of villages and their relationships help us understand a homeland as a place of movement, kinship, and shared life.

rows.title: Merrick Neck in Historical Records
rows.summary: Merrack Neck appears in a 1658 record, preserving an early form of the Merrick name in the South Shore landscape.
rows.address_label: Merrick Neck documentary reference; village location unconfirmed
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Linked to Merrick Ancestral Land as a south shore community and bay landscape.
rows.why_this_matters: Names such as Merrack Neck carry traces of an older coastal geography into the present. They connect familiar South Shore places with the Native history behind the Merrick name.

rows.title: Merrick Road: Ancient South Shore Trail
rows.summary: The modern road corridor preserves continuity between Indigenous movement, colonial travel, and today's everyday route.
rows.address_label: Merrick Road / South Country Road corridor, Freeport-Baldwin-Merrick area
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Linked to Merrick Ancestral Land as a south shore travel corridor.
rows.why_this_matters: Merrick Road shows how everyday infrastructure can preserve traces of older Native geographies. Seen as a south shore travel corridor, the road carries histories of movement, exchange, and connection across Merrick ancestral land.

rows.title: Merrick and Massapequa: A Local Account of Refuge
rows.summary: A Baldwin local history remembers Massapequa people offering refuge to Merrick families displaced by colonial settlement.
rows.address_label: Regional Merrick–Massapequa history; no identified parcel
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Linked to Merrick Ancestral Land with recognition of overlapping Merikoke/Merrick and Massapequa histories.
rows.why_this_matters: Displacement also brought people into relationships of refuge and support. This local account remembers connections between neighboring Native communities during colonial expansion.

rows.title: Merricks
rows.summary: Merrick territory is remembered across the southern part of Long Island, from the Rockville Centre area toward the western Oyster Bay line, with ties to necks, bays, and south-shore places. Older histories say the Merrick people moved east from the western end of Long Island into a landscape shaped by Massapequa power and tribute relationships. Those accounts are colonial-era interpretations; Merrick place names, community presence, and documented land relationships remain the focus here.

rows.title: Messemennuck (Peconic Bay)
rows.summary: Messemennuck is a Peconic Bay and river-boundary placename associated with alewife fishing and the western bounds of Shinnecock territory.

rows.title: Messtopass (Mannatto Hill)
rows.summary: Messtopass is documented as a boundary landmark near Mannatto Hill in the town of Oyster Bay. A Huntington place-name source places it on the western boundary south of Old Country Road.

rows.title: Miamegg (Jamesport Creek)
rows.summary: Miamegg is a Jamesport creek placename connected with a 1648 deed and interpreted as a meeting fishing-place.
rows.address_label: Kings Creek / Hawks Creek, South Jamesport, Riverhead, NY (approximate waterway orientation)

rows.title: Mica Tablet Site
rows.summary: In 1849, New York State received a mica plate reportedly found while plowing in Brookhaven. Engraved geometric and other figures make the object unusual, but its exact findspot, age, and cultural interpretation remain uncertain.
rows.activity_update_summary: Restored the New York State Museum photograph of the Mica Tablet and strengthened the public explanation of its uncertain provenance, interpretation, and Unkechaug landscape context.
rows.why_this_matters: Chief Harry Wallace's oral history connects the broader Fireplace Neck landscape with Unkechaug whaling, community life, and ancestral responsibility. Reading the tablet beside that living history preserves the object's cultural context while leaving its exact age, findspot, and meaning explicitly uncertain.

rows.title: Milburn Creek and Bedell's Landing Vicinity
rows.summary: Milburn Creek and the Bedell's Landing area are part of a wider Freeport-Baldwin shoreline landscape where local histories remember Merrick maritime life, shellfishing, wampum-making materials, and stone implements found near the creek.
rows.address_label: Milburn Pond Park / Milburn Creek Park, West Merrick Road and South Brookside Avenue, Freeport, NY
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Within and near Merrick ancestral land; connected to the broader creek-and-bay landscape.
rows.why_this_matters: Milburn Creek carries the history of Meroke fishing and shoreline life alongside later changes to the waterway. Looking from today’s public park connects that longer history with the ponds, roads and neighborhoods people know now.

rows.title: Minasseroke (Strong's Neck)
rows.summary: Minasseroke is connected with Little Neck, now Strong's Neck, at Setauket. The neck lies between Conscience Bay and Setauket Harbor and is associated in local history with Setalcott presence and a place remembered as Indian Ground.
rows.listing_image_alt: Strongs Neck Site Setauket, or Indian Ground Site_5I5A0316 WEB

rows.title: Minnahanonck (Roosevelt Island)
rows.summary: Minnahanonck is connected with Blackwell's Island in the East River, the island now known as Roosevelt Island. The name appears in early New Netherland sources connected with Marychtenwikingh people from present-day Brooklyn.

rows.title: Minnapaugs (Horton's Point Pond)
rows.summary: William Wallace Tooker links Minnapaugs with a small freshwater pond by Long Island Sound at Horton's Point in Southold. The place also appears in Hashamomuk Neck boundary language, tying the pond to a wider named landscape west of Greenport.

rows.title: Minnesunk (North Sea Pond)
rows.summary: Minnesunk is a modern name applied to a pond at North Sea in Southampton, not an older Long Island Indigenous placename. It shows how later writers sometimes created Native-sounding names from mixed or imported language material.

rows.title: Minnisais (Liberty Island)
rows.summary: Minnisais is a Chippewa name applied by Henry R. Schoolcraft to Bedlow's Island, now Liberty Island. It is included here as a later introduced name, not an older local placename from Long Island or New York Harbor records.

rows.title: Mispatuck / Masquetux
rows.summary: A West Islip placename cluster linking Mispatuck, Mispotuck, Misputuck, Masquetux, neck land, brook geography, and older boundary language.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Secatogue Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Missi Kesukut
rows.summary: Shinnecock advocates worked for decades to protect an archaeologically sensitive area in Water Mill from development. Their efforts shaped excavation safeguards, care for ancestral remains, and a later public preservation effort while keeping the exact sensitive location off the public map.
rows.address_label: Montauk Highway, Water Mill
rows.why_this_matters: Shinnecock intervention changed how Southampton Town handled archaeology, ancestral remains, and development in Water Mill. The history demonstrates that preservation depends on Native authority and sustained community advocacy, not only on what construction or excavation happens to uncover.

rows.title: Missing Meroke Village Marker, Merrick
rows.summary: A former New York State historic marker in Merrick acknowledged a Meroke village area. It is no longer standing, but its text keeps local memory of Meroke presence visible.
rows.address_label: Sunrise Highway vicinity, west of Central Boulevard, Merrick
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Meroke is one of the historical forms associated with the Merrick name.
rows.why_this_matters: The missing Meroke marker shows how Native place history can be acknowledged in one generation and fade from the roadside landscape in another. Restoring the story helps reconnect Merrick to Meroke presence while treating village places with respect.

rows.title: Missipaug (Big Fresh Pond)
rows.summary: Missipaug is listed as a name suggested for Big Fresh Pond near North Sea. The name points to a real Southampton pond while also showing how some Native-sounding Long Island names were created or regularized by later writers.
rows.address_label: Big Fresh Pond, North Sea, Southampton, NY

rows.title: Mogkompskut (Great Rock)
rows.summary: Mogkompskut names a large boulder in the Hands Creek Road and Three Mile Harbor area of East Hampton. William Wallace Tooker preserved the name from Stephen Pharaoh of the Montaukett Tribe.
rows.address_label: Hands Creek Road near Three Mile Harbor, East Hampton, NY

rows.title: Molly's Hill
rows.summary: Molly's Hill is a remembered Montaukett place near the meeting of Fireplace Road and Gerard Drive in Springs. Jacqueline Overton's 1963 local history associates the hill with Molly Pharoah and the early life of her son, Stephen Talkhouse Pharoah. Later road construction altered the hill and its surrounding landscape.

rows.title: Momoweta Pond (Laurel Lake)
rows.summary: Momoweta Pond, now known as Laurel Lake, is a North Fork waterbody named for Momoweta, sachem of Corchaug.
rows.address_label: Laurel Lake, Laurel / Mattituck, Southold, NY

rows.title: Monabaugs (Westhampton)
rows.summary: Monabaugs names a creek, swamp, and pond in the Westhampton area between Potunk and Ketchaponack Necks. The history preserves a water-place name in a landscape where coastal wetlands and waterways have changed over time.
rows.address_label: Westhampton area between Potunk and Ketchaponack Necks, Southampton, NY

rows.title: Montauk Auction Landscape (1879)
rows.summary: In 1879, a court-ordered auction transferred the Montauk proprietors’ holdings to Brooklyn businessman Arthur Benson. Montaukett families still held rights in their homeland. The sale was followed by pressure to leave Indian Fields, broken promises, and a long struggle over land and recognition.
rows.address_label: Approximate historical landscape — not a visitor entrance
rows.why_this_matters: A colonial land record describes a claim made at a particular time. Read its conditions and the people affected alongside the map; an outlined claim is not proof that Native relationships or rights ended.

rows.title: Montaukett Ancestral Land
rows.summary: Montauk is a living Montaukett homeland, with deep ancestral ties to its waters, Indian Fields and places beyond the East End. Dispossession and a 1910 court declaration of extinction did not end the people. Montaukett families continue community and cultural work and the campaign to restore state recognition. Montaukett ancestry also lives within the Brothertown Indian Nation in Wisconsin, connecting this homeland to a wider history of kinship and survival.
rows.listing_image_alt: 1879 public auction map of Montauk lands.
rows.activity_update_summary: Consolidated the dated 1470–2025 Montaukett history and its repeated image into the cited Historic Timeline after repairing all moment links to this published ancestral-land page.
rows.why_this_matters: Montaukett Ancestral Land is a living homeland story, not only an East End place name. It connects language, fortified high land, shoreline movement, leadership, land loss, and continued Montaukett presence.

rows.title: Montaukett Indian Museum
rows.summary: A museum at Second House in Montauk, where collections, contested authority over Native history, and Native leadership meet. David Bunn Martine’s appointment as director was reported in October 2026.
rows.address_label: Second House grounds, 12 Second House Road, Montauk, NY
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Public museum on Montaukett ancestral land; operated by the Montauk Historical Society.
rows.why_this_matters: Native people are more than the subjects of museum displays. This place connects the history of collecting with ongoing questions of consent, interpretation, and community authority. Martine’s leadership offers visitors a way to encounter Montaukett continuity through a Native artist and museum professional, while the institution’s earlier debates remain part of its history.

rows.title: Moriches
rows.summary: Moriches is a south-shore Brookhaven placename connected with a neck of land at Unquichoge and with the later hamlets of Moriches, Center Moriches, and East Moriches. Early forms include Merquices and Meritche.

rows.title: Mosquetah (Mosquito Cove)
rows.summary: Mosquetah is a Glen Cove placename remembered in the later English form Mosquito Cove. The name refers to meadows or rushes along the cove or creek, not to the insect.

rows.title: Munchog (Great Pond Island)
rows.summary: A Montauk island name in Great Pond, now Lake Montauk, connected with older forms such as Munchoage and Manchoage.

rows.title: Munnawtawkit (Fishers Island)
rows.summary: Munnawtawkit names Fishers Island, an island politically within Southold though closer to Connecticut. The name is connected with Pequot fishing and planting and with other eastern island and high-land names.

rows.title: Muskyttehool (Flatlands)
rows.summary: Muskyttehool is a Flatlands, Kings County placename for a pool or wet place where rushes grew. The popular Musquito hole explanation is best understood as a misunderstanding of a rush-place name.

rows.title: Musquatax / Squorums Neck
rows.summary: Musquatax names a creek on Mastic Neck in Brookhaven. The cited source places it within Unkechaug land-title geography and interprets the name as a rush-growing place.

rows.title: Nachaquatuck (Cold Spring Harbor Creek)
rows.summary: Nachaquatuck names the creek or river at Cold Spring Harbor that marked Huntington's western boundary, linking the placename to boundary language and tidal-stream geography.

rows.title: Naghtognk (Corlears Hook)
rows.summary: A Manhattan placename for Corlears Hook, linked with Dutch forms Nechtauk and Nechtank and interpreted as a landmark-tree name.

rows.title: Nameoke (Rockaway)
rows.summary: Nameoke names a traditional locality near Rockaway village in old Hempstead town. The name is interpreted as a fishing-place name rather than a phrase meaning water edge.

rows.title: Nanemoset (Wading River Brook)
rows.summary: Nanemoset is a recorded Indigenous brook name whose exact location remains uncertain. William Wallace Tooker tentatively associated it with Wading River or a tributary, drawing on a 1663 Setauket land agreement and related names in Brookhaven records.

rows.title: Napock (Peconic River Headwaters)
rows.summary: Napock is connected with the Peconic River headwaters, a chain of ponds and wetlands along the Riverhead/Brookhaven boundary. The history preserves a boundary placename tied to water, pools, and the interior landscape of central Long Island. The name is interpreted as a water-place or pool-place.

rows.title: Narrioch (Gravesend Neck)
rows.summary: Narrioch is a Kings County placename associated with Gravesend Neck, interpreted as a point or corner of land. The name is tied to the same 1654 release that names Mannahanning.

rows.title: Nassakeag (South Setauket)
rows.summary: Nassakeag is connected with the southwest border of Setauket in Brookhaven town, in the locality later known as South Setauket. The name is tied both to a swamp and to Nassakeag, a Nissequogue sachem whose name appears in regional land records.

rows.title: Native American Greenway at Lister Park
rows.summary: A public marker beside the Mill River introduces Native histories of fishing, seasonal movement, and colonial displacement in the Rockville Centre landscape.
rows.address_label: Lister Park, Riverside Road entrance, Rockville Centre
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Merikoke and neighboring communities are remembered along the Mill River.
rows.why_this_matters: A familiar riverside park can also be a place to learn whose histories shaped the landscape. The sign provides a concrete starting point for reading the Mill River alongside Native communities and colonial displacement.

rows.title: Nayack (Fort Hamilton)
rows.summary: Nayack is connected with the New Utrecht point of land at present-day Fort Hamilton, directly opposite Staten Island. The history preserves a western Long Island shore name tied to the Narrows and the New Netherland period.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Canarsie Traditional Land on the current ancestral territory map.
rows.why_this_matters: Danckaerts’ 1679 visit shows Nayack families farming, cooking and working on a corner of land they had to rent back from the man who bought it.

rows.title: Nayantacawnick (Probable Fishers Island)
rows.summary: Nayantacawnick is the island name Roger Williams used in 1637 while discussing the forced placement of captive Pequot families. Historical place-name sources interpret it as being opposite Niantic and identify Fishers Island as the most likely modern location, while also naming Plum Island as an alternative.
rows.address_label: Fishers Island, Town of Southold, NY (probable broad identification)
rows.why_this_matters: Nayantacawnick preserves a seventeenth-century regional name while also documenting a proposal to confine Pequot families after war. Mapping the probable island makes that history visible, and retaining the uncertainty prevents a geographic inference from being presented as settled fact.

rows.title: Neapeague (Napeague Beach)
rows.summary: Neapeague, now commonly Napeague, is the sandy and marshy water-land connecting Montauk with the main part of Long Island in East Hampton town.

rows.title: Neckapauge (Green's Creek)
rows.summary: Neckapauge is associated with Green's Creek, west of Sayville in the Town of Islip. The name appears in connection with the eastern boundary and beginning bound of the Nicoll Patent.

rows.title: Neguntatogue (Lindenhurst)
rows.summary: Neguntatogue is associated with a neck of land south of Breslau, now Lindenhurst, between Little Neck and Santapogue.
rows.address_label: Neguntatogue Neck / Venetian Shores, Lindenhurst, NY (broad public orientation)

rows.title: Nesaquaque Accompsett
rows.summary: The name is interpreted as land on the other side of Nissequogue, tying Smithtown west-river geography to Fresh Pond and older place-name records.
rows.address_label: West side of the Nissequogue River toward Fresh Pond, Kings Park, NY (broad public orientation)

rows.title: Nesconset / Nasseconset
rows.summary: Nasseconset is connected with a Nissequogue sachem and with the modern hamlet name Nesconset in Smithtown. The name belongs to the Nissequogue River and Smithtown regional landscape, where personal names and land names often overlap in colonial records.

rows.title: Newtown: Settlement, War and Reserved Native Rights
rows.summary: Newtown was a colonial town in western Queens, centered near present-day Elmhurst. English settlers obtained Dutch government grants, then further Native agreements under English rule. Named officials and settlers expanded claims over land where Native rights had remained reserved.
rows.address_label: Approximate historical landscape — not a visitor entrance
rows.why_this_matters: Colonial grants and Native land agreements were different acts. Their sequence shows how settlement expanded, while reserved rights and continuing communities challenge a story of simple disappearance.

rows.title: Niamuck / Merosuck (Canoe Place)
rows.summary: Niamuck and Merosuck are recorded names connected with Canoe Place in Southampton, the narrow isthmus between Shinnecock Bay and Peconic Bay. The place is central to Shinnecock geography and to the portage route later cut by the Shinnecock Canal.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Shinnecock Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
rows.why_this_matters: Canoe Place preserves the memory of an Indigenous portage route connecting two bays. Showing Niamuck and Merosuck together keeps both recorded names searchable while making clear that they describe the same broader landscape rather than two separate sites.

rows.title: Nippaug (Little Fresh Pond)
rows.summary: Nippaug is a later suggested Algonquian-style name for Little Fresh Pond, kept here with caution because the naming history differs from older local placename records.
rows.address_label: Little Fresh Pond, North Sea, Southampton, NY

rows.title: Nipscop (Conkling's Farm)
rows.summary: Nipscop is recorded as a traditional name for Conkling's Farm, a tract in the western part of Islip town and partly in Babylon. The history preserves a local name attached to a farm landscape whose exact modern bounds require review. The name's meaning remains uncertain.

rows.title: Nissequogue (Smithtown)
rows.summary: A Smithtown-area name preserved in Dutch and English forms, including Nisinckqueghacky and Nesequake.

rows.title: Nissequogue / Wissiquack River
rows.summary: Wissiquack is recorded as a corrupted form of Nissequogue in Smithtown and belongs with the Tackan/Nissequogue discussion.

rows.title: Nissequogue Ancestral Land
rows.summary: The Nissequogue River preserves a Native name within an ancestral homeland shaped by generations of life along its waters. Colonial deeds and the growth of Smithtown narrowed Native control, but those documents do not tell the whole story of the people. Matinecock and Setalcott communities remain present on this North Shore; their histories remind us that family relationships reach beyond the separate territories shown on a map.
rows.why_this_matters: Nissequogue Ancestral Land places the river and North Shore within Native geography. Place names, waterways, and boundary records carry evidence of Native presence, diplomacy, and land pressure across generations.

rows.title: Nobbs (Goose Creek)
rows.summary: Nobbs is a Flanders-area placename associated with Goose Creek, one of the creeks named in Paucamp's testimony about the west end of Peconic Bay.
rows.address_label: Goose Creek, Flanders, NY

rows.title: Noccomack (West Mastic Meadows)
rows.summary: Noccomack is connected with meadows and land on the west side of Mastic Neck in Brookhaven. The recorded forms point to a wetland place between upland and bay on the Mastic Peninsula.

rows.title: Nominick Hills
rows.summary: Nominick is connected with hills on Montauk in East Hampton, where the high land rises out of the sandy and marshy Neapeague. The placename is remembered through traditional usage and later local writing rather than early town records.

rows.title: Nonowantuck (Crystal Brook)
rows.summary: Nonowantuck preserves a remembered Indigenous name for a creek in the Mount Sinai landscape. William Wallace Tooker associated it with Crystal Brook, a stream and valley on the harbor’s western side, while acknowledging that he had found no early written forms of the name.
rows.why_this_matters: A creek can disappear or change while its name preserves knowledge of the landscape. Nonowantuck invites us to read Mount Sinai through Indigenous place naming as well as later English names, and to distinguish what a historical source records from what remains uncertain.

rows.title: North Fork: Colonial Claims and Continuing Native Rights
rows.summary: Southold’s English officials used confirming deeds and a colonial patent to consolidate claims across the North Fork. Native signers, reserved rights and later objections show a process of dispossession, not one uncontested sale.
rows.address_label: Wading River through Orient — regional historical context
rows.why_this_matters: A colonial patent could claim town jurisdiction without proving that all Native land had been acquired. Native names, reservations and disputes reveal continuing rights and the people whose lives a broad grant could obscure.

rows.title: North Merrick Descendant Community Landscape
rows.summary: North Merrick lies beside the former Hempstead commons, where Native and Black residents depended on shared access to land. The history of enclosure and displacement connects this landscape with wider struggles over work, belonging, and the resources needed to sustain a community.
rows.address_label: North Merrick area, Town of Hempstead
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Linked to Merrick Ancestral Land as a Native descendant-community learning point.
rows.why_this_matters: North Merrick's Native descendant history shows that Merrick survivance continued through family networks, adaptation, labor, landholding, and community memory. The neighborhood is presented as a broad landscape of Native continuity after land loss.

rows.title: North Neck Burial Ground Rally
rows.summary: The North Neck Burial Ground Rally brought Montaukett families, Shinnecock supporters, singers, and allies together to defend an eighteenth-century Montaukett burial ground connected with Cyrus Charles.
rows.address_label: North Neck, Montauk (generalized)
rows.why_this_matters: This stop shows intercommunity support and public ceremony as part of burial-ground defense.

rows.title: Nowedonah (Lake Nowedonah / Mill Pond)
rows.summary: Nowedonah is the name of a Shinnecock sachem and was later given to Mill Pond at Water Mill. The placename preserves a connection between the Water Mill pond and Shinnecock leadership remembered in seventeenth-century records.

rows.title: Noyack (Jessup's Neck)
rows.summary: Noyack is associated with Noyack Bay, the hamlet now often spelled Noyac, and the long point or neck of land known as Jessup's Neck. The area also has archaeological evidence of long Indigenous use, including village and procurement-site contexts around Noyack.

rows.title: Opcatkontycke Creek
rows.summary: Opcatkontycke names a brook at Northport in Huntington. The name appears in the first Huntington purchase, where the stream formed the eastern boundary of the tract opposite Nachaquetack at Cold Spring Harbor.

rows.title: Operhoweseck / Opechowseck Brook
rows.summary: An Indigenous brook name preserved in Huntington’s 1687 records shows how waterways became reference points in colonial claims to land.
rows.address_label: Present-day Huntington / Halesite, NY
rows.why_this_matters: Indigenous names remain embedded in documents written to organize colonial ownership. Following this brook’s name helps distinguish the remembered landscape from the legal claims later imposed on it.

rows.title: Orient Burial
rows.summary: The Orient Site is one of four known Orient Period (1,300 - 1,000 BC) burials on eastern Long Island. The cultural period receives its name from the fish shaped projectile points with distinct shoulders. During this period, the areas used for ceremonial burials were greatly removed from habitation areas, suggesting a reverence for their preservation. Oral stories support this hypothesis.
rows.address_label: Main Road, Orient area

rows.title: Osprey Road Burial Site Confrontation
rows.summary: After construction exposed a Native group burial on Shelter Island in October 2003, Shinnecock community members pressed town officials for respect, consultation, and stronger protection of ancestral remains. The confrontation became part of a broader effort to improve burial-protection law.
rows.address_label: Shelter Island Town Board, Shelter Island (site generalized)
rows.why_this_matters: Shinnecock advocates turned the disturbance of ancestors into a public demand for consultation, respect, and stronger burial-protection law.

rows.title: Ouheywichkingh (Unkechaug village)
rows.summary: Ouheywichkingh is a Dutch-recorded form for an Unkechaug village near Mastic Neck in Brookhaven. The name belongs with the wider Unkechaug place-name record, but it is preserved here because the 1645 treaty form is distinct and historically important.

rows.title: Oyster Bay and Glen Cove: Colonial Patents and Native Land
rows.summary: English governor Edmund Andros claimed town-wide authority for Oyster Bay in 1677 while acknowledging Native land within its boundaries that had not yet been purchased. Separate agreements and resource rights show why this region cannot be explained as one completed sale.
rows.address_label: Oyster Bay, Glen Cove and coastal islands — modern regional context
rows.why_this_matters: The patent itself acknowledged Native land that had not been purchased. Naming the English government and settlers behind the claim makes visible how colonial authority could spread beyond particular agreements, without treating a map outline as proof of Native consent or disappearance.

rows.title: Oyster Bay: A Native Agreement and Expanding Colonial Claims
rows.summary: Asiapum/Mohenes and three English purchasers are named in Oyster Bay’s 1653 agreement. Rivers, an excluded island, settler allotments and later boundary disputes reveal how colonial claims expanded across a Native landscape whose Matinecock connections continue.
rows.address_label: Northern Nassau regional history — not a visitor entrance
rows.why_this_matters: A purchase date alone cannot explain the transfer of power. Named parties, excluded land, measured settler allotments and official recording show how a written claim worked, while Matinecock cultural work makes clear that the people did not disappear.

rows.title: Pagganck / Governors Island
rows.summary: Pagganck is the name recorded for modern Governors Island in a June 16, 1637 deed. The record names Cacapeteyno and Pewihas as owners acting with the consent of their community at Keshaechquereren and conveys the island to Wouter van Twiller. Later sources also preserve the spelling Pagganch.
rows.address_label: Governors Island, New York Harbor, New York, NY (historic northern island footprint)

rows.title: Pantigo
rows.summary: Pantigo names a locality between East Hampton village and Amagansett. The place is also associated with Pantigo Hill, where a seventeenth-century Montaukett cemetery was documented in the early twentieth century.

rows.title: Papequatunck
rows.summary: Papequatunck is an Oyster Bay placename from a 1653 deed, interpreted as opened or broken-up land and associated with Native planting ground west of Oyster Bay River. Papequatunck is an Oyster Bay placename preserved in the first Indian deed for Oyster Bay. The name marks the western side of the land description and is associated with land cleared for Native planting.

rows.title: Paquatuck (Terrell River)
rows.summary: Paquatuck names the creek or tidal river now known as Terrell River, on the line between East Moriches and Center Moriches in Brookhaven. The name appears in colonial boundary language for Moriches Neck.

rows.title: Pascu-ucks
rows.summary: Pascu-ucks is connected with a creek on the island historically called Screcunkas, now associated with Cedar Island in Babylon's Great South Bay.

rows.title: Passasqueung / Arrasquaug
rows.summary: Passasqueung and Arrasquaug are connected with a creek at South Oyster Bay, now associated in the source with Minell's Creek.

rows.title: Passquessit (East End of Fishers Island)
rows.summary: Passquessit is a placename for the east end of Fishers Island, an adjacent island in the Town of Southold.

rows.title: Patchogue
rows.summary: Patchogue is a Brookhaven placename connected with Pochoug Neck, local stream geography, and later village history on the south shore of Long Island.

rows.title: Patchummuck (Tom's Creek)
rows.summary: Patchummuck is connected with a boundary point at the head of Tom's Creek on Hashamomuk Neck in Southold.

rows.title: Pattersquash Island
rows.summary: An island in Narrow Bay, between Mastic Beach and Fire Island, within Unkechaug homelands. Its name also appears in records of nearby mainland creeks, meadows, and land.

rows.title: Patuckquapaug
rows.summary: Patuckquapaug, located on the edge of what is now known as Round Pond in Sag Harbor, was once a village site for what was likely a subgroup of the Shinnecock.

rows.title: Paucuckatux (Tom's Creek)
rows.summary: Paucuckatux is identified as a creek on the bounds of Hashamomuk Neck in Southold, probably the stream known as Tom's Creek.

rows.title: Paumanack / Eastern Long Island
rows.summary: Paumanack is a broad Indigenous placename documented for Eastern Long Island, not a single village, creek, neck, or pond. Its marker is a representative regional label rather than a boundary.
rows.address_label: Eastern Long Island (representative map label near Riverhead / Peconic)
rows.why_this_matters: Paumanack names Eastern Long Island at a regional scale and keeps Indigenous political and geographic relationships visible beyond modern town boundaries. The representative marker invites visitors to read the linked records without reducing a broad homeland to one exact coordinate.

rows.title: Pauquacumsuck / Pahquahkossit (Wading River)
rows.summary: Wading River’s Indigenous name connects the creek with quahog gathering and Native knowledge of the coastal landscape. Paucamp’s 1660 testimony preserves that connection, while later Native-led church history shows community life continuing beyond the colonial deeds.

rows.title: Payaquotusk (Pipe's Neck)
rows.summary: Payaquotusk is a Southold placename for Pipe's Neck in the Arshamomaque and Hashamomuk Neck landscape.

rows.title: Peacepunck (West Branch of Nissequogue River)
rows.summary: Peacepunck names the west branch of the Nissequogue River in Smithtown, where a partition division among Richard Smith's heirs described a branch south of the mills.
rows.address_label: Nissequogue River / Blydenburgh County Park, Smithtown, NY (broad waterway orientation)

rows.title: Peconic
rows.summary: Peconic is a long-running eastern Long Island placename now associated with the Peconic River, Peconic Bay, and the hamlet of Peconic.

rows.title: Pell Site
rows.summary: In 1997, the Pell case began, involving an attempt to steal Shinnecock Reservation land. On a strip of land south of Montauk Highway and the Tide Water Pub, the Shinnecock tribe successfully defended the land from being taken and developed.

rows.title: Penataquit Creek (Bay Shore)
rows.summary: Penataquit is a Bay Shore placename associated with Penataquit Creek and with older boundary language for Aweeksa Neck in Islip.

rows.title: Pequash (Goldsmith's Neck)
rows.summary: Pequash is a Cutchogue placename for a neck of land known as Goldsmith's Neck, interpreted as open or cleared ground.

rows.title: Pesapunck
rows.summary: Pesapunck is a Southold placename for a neck and meadow between Cutchogue and Mattituck, interpreted as a hot house or sweat lodge place.

rows.title: Plum Island: Competing Claims and a Continuing Montaukett Voice
rows.summary: Wyandanch, Samuel Wyllys, Southold townsmen and English governor Edmund Andros appear in competing claims to Plum Island. The history continues in the Montaukett Indian Nation’s call to participate in decisions about the island’s future.
rows.address_label: Plum Island, off Orient Point — modern main-island outline
rows.why_this_matters: Who gets to decide what happens to a homeland? Colonial deeds, town divisions, manor authority and federal ownership changed control of Plum Island. The Montaukett Indian Nation’s call for consultation shows why conservation planning must also reckon with Native relationships and authority.

rows.title: Pomiches Creek (East Moriches)
rows.summary: Pomiches is an East Moriches creek placename remembered as the western boundary of Watchogue Neck and interpreted as a crossing or crossway.

rows.title: Ponquogue / Bondyquogue
rows.summary: Ponquogue is represented as a Hampton Bays placename with Bondyquogue kept as a related spelling or cross-reference form. The blue marker gives a modern orientation near Ponquogue Bridge.

rows.title: Poquatuck (Orient Point / Long Beach Bay)
rows.summary: Poquatuck is an Orient Point and Long Beach Bay placename in Southold, interpreted as a clear or open tidal cove or creek.

rows.title: Poquott (Dyer's Neck)
rows.summary: Poquott is a traditional placename for Dyer's Neck between Setauket and Port Jefferson, interpreted as clear land or open country but treated cautiously by Tooker.

rows.title: Potinack
rows.summary: Potinack is a Montauk placename for a hole or deep depression in the Hither Plains and Hither Woods landscape, with related watering-place references at Montauk and Amagansett.
rows.listing_image_alt: Potinack, Napeague Bay archaeological landscape and corn fields
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Montaukett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Potunk Neck (Westhampton)
rows.summary: Potunk is a Westhampton placename for Potunk Neck and nearby meadowland, recorded in seventeenth-century Southampton and East Hampton references and interpreted as a boggy place.

rows.title: Poxabog / Poxabogue Pond
rows.summary: Poxabogue preserves an Indigenous pond name in Sagaponack, connecting changing water levels with the language recorded in Southampton’s colonial land surveys.
rows.address_label: Present-day Sagaponack, near Bridgehampton, NY
rows.why_this_matters: A pond’s changing shoreline can help us understand why a place name mattered. Poxabogue links an Indigenous name preserved in land records with a wetland landscape people can still learn from today.

rows.title: Poyhas Swamp
rows.summary: Poyhas is recorded as a swamp within the Hashamomuk bounds in Southold. The place is connected with Poyhas, a Native person who lived and planted there.
rows.address_label: Hashamomuck Neck, Southold, NY (broad wetland orientation)

rows.title: Preservation Long Island
rows.summary: Preservation Long Island worked with Indigenous artists and guest curators to present Indigenous History & Art at Good Little Water Place in 2020. The online exhibition brought contemporary Native art into conversation with Long Island land, water, wildlife, history, and community.
rows.address_label: 161 West Main Street, Cold Spring Harbor, NY 11724
rows.listing_image_alt: Painting by Shinnecock artist David Bunn Martine, on view at Preservation Long Island as part of Indigenous History & Art at Good Little Water Place (2020).
rows.why_this_matters: References: Preservation Long Island, "Virtual Exhibition: Indigenous History & Art at Good Little Water Place," July 31, 2020, preservationlongisland.org; Indigenous History & Art at Good Little Water Place, About, indigenoushistoryandart.omeka.net.

rows.title: Prospect Park — Lenape Ridge and Road
rows.summary: Prospect Park lies in Lenapehoking. Lenape families planted the Flatbush lands beside an ancient road that is now Flatbush Avenue. Colonial seizure, war and removal followed, but Native Brooklyn continues, from Lefferts Historic House to neighborhoods across the borough.
rows.address_label: Prospect Park Boathouse, 101 East Drive, on the Lullwater, Brooklyn, NY
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Canarsie Traditional Land on the current ancestral territory map.
rows.why_this_matters: Prospect Park looks like countryside, but its ridge, road and planting lands are Lenape places. A walk from Battle Pass to Lefferts Historic House follows that history from Lenape fields to colonial seizure, war and Lenape return.

rows.title: Pumcatawe
rows.summary: Pumcatawe is recorded as a small tract of land and meadow east of Mastic River in Brookhaven. The name is connected with a Native person who formerly lived on the land.

rows.title: Pung-Plues Creek
rows.summary: Pung-Plues is recorded as a small creek at Moriches in Brookhaven. In a 1681 deed, it formed the western boundary of a small neck of land and meadow near Watchogue and the bay.

rows.title: Punk's Hole (Manorville)
rows.summary: Punk's Hole was a former name for the village known as Manor, now associated with Manorville, or for a nearby hollow. The name combines a local hollow with punk, an Algonquian word used for fungus or tinder from old oak trees and stumps.

rows.title: Quadams Hill
rows.summary: Quadams is recorded as a hill in the Indian Field near Oyster Pond at Montauk. The name appears to preserve a personal name attached to a feature in the Montaukett landscape.
rows.address_label: Montauk County Park west of Oyster Pond, Montauk, NY (broad public orientation)

rows.title: Quagga Path
rows.summary: Quagga, also written Quogo or Quago, is recorded as an Indian trail or path in western Southampton at Atlanticville, now the East Quogue area. The name was used for a path leading toward Quaquanantuck Neck and the meadows.

rows.title: Qualican
rows.summary: Qualican is recorded as a locality on Mastic Neck in Brookhaven. The name appears in the 1700 William Smith deed connected with lands for the Unkechaug people at Pusspatok.

rows.title: Quanch Island
rows.summary: Quanch is recorded as an island in Great South Bay opposite Bellport in Brookhaven. The name appears in a town-record description involving meadowland and Whale House Point.

rows.title: Quandoequareous (Newtown Creek)
rows.summary: A Queens creek-name for the west branch of Newtown Creek, connected in older records with the Mespat kills.
rows.address_label: Maspeth Creek / western Newtown Creek, Queens, NY (approximate waterway orientation)

rows.title: Quanuntowunk (Fort Pond)
rows.summary: A Montauk deed placename pairing Fort Pond geography with Konkhunganik and showing how north and south pond-side places were recorded together.
rows.address_label: Northern Fort Pond, Montauk, NY (broad water orientation)

rows.title: Quaquanantuck / Quantuck Bay and Creek
rows.summary: A western Southampton creek, bay, meadow, and purchase-record name preserved in seventeenth-century sources.

rows.title: Quarapin (Round Swamp)
rows.summary: A Huntington swamp placename remembered as the planting place of a Native person named Quarapin.

rows.title: Quggalune
rows.summary: Quggalune is recorded as a locality in western Southampton, in the Quoquanantuck or Quogue purchase landscape near Assop's Neck.

rows.title: Quiogue
rows.summary: Quiogue is recorded as a neck of land between Aspatuck and Quantuck creeks in western Southampton. The place was formerly known as Little Assop's Neck.

rows.title: Quogue
rows.summary: Quogue is recorded as a village in western Southampton on Quantuck Bay. The name is a shortened form of Quaquanantuck, the older name for the salt meadows and land in this section.

rows.title: Quogue Historical Society — Shinnecock Family History
rows.summary: A public museum and research collection preserving Quogue history, including the Enos family and the Shinnecock Arms.
rows.address_label: Pond House, 114 Jessup Avenue, Quogue, NY 11959
rows.why_this_matters: Read alongside family records, the 1938 Shinnecock Arms listing shows how local history reaches beyond buildings and place names into work, hospitality and the barriers travelers faced. Keeping these records accessible makes those relationships part of Quogue’s public history.

rows.title: Quonettquott
rows.summary: Quonettquott is connected with the West Connecticut River, known as Connetquot Brook in Islip. The name is interpreted as at the long river.
rows.address_label: Connetquot River State Park Preserve, Oakdale, NY (waterway orientation)

rows.title: Raconkamuck / Lake Ronkonkoma
rows.summary: Raconkamuck, now Lake Ronkonkoma, is a central Long Island freshwater lake on the bounds of Brookhaven, Islip, and Smithtown. The name is interpreted as a boundary or fence fishing-place.
rows.address_label: Lake Ronkonkoma, Suffolk County, NY (waterbody orientation)

rows.title: Rapahamuck
rows.summary: Rapahamuck appears in western Southampton records around Flanders, Birch Creek, and the Aquebaug meadow allotments. The name is tied to a neck, a point and an island, so its place on the map is general, not one exact spot.
rows.address_label: Birch Creek area, Flanders, NY

rows.title: Rassapeague
rows.summary: A Stony Brook Harbor swamp, meadow, and bay placename interpreted as a muddy or miry water place.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Setauket Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Reeve Farm Site
rows.summary: The Reeve Farm Site is remembered through the disturbance, collection, and public display of Native ancestral remains uncovered in Aquebogue in 1961. The episode shows how farming, collecting, archaeological interpretation, and museum display harmed Native ancestors and why burial protection remains necessary.

rows.title: Rev. Paul Cuffee Gravesite
rows.summary: A single fenced grave marks the burial location of Reverend Paul Cuffee, a Shinnecock minister connected with the old Native church meeting place at Good Ground, now Hampton Bays. Cuffee followed the religious path of his grandfather Peter John and preached among Native communities on Long Island.
rows.address_label: Good Ground Road area
