rows.activity_update_summary: Kept the related-biography context and consolidated the dated Rev. Paul Cuffee history and images into the cited Historic Timeline.

rows.title: Rinnegackonck
rows.summary: Rinnegackonck is a Brooklyn placename associated with the plantation of George Rapaljee and early Dutch records near western Long Island.

rows.title: Roanoke Point
rows.summary: Roanoke is recorded as a point of land on the north shore of Long Island in Riverhead town. The source cautions that it was probably adopted from Roanoke in Virginia rather than being an original Long Island Indigenous name.

rows.title: Rockaway
rows.summary: Rockaway is a place-name associated with the Rockaway Peninsula and the Rockaway people. The name is recorded in seventeenth-century deeds and is interpreted as referring to sandy land or country.

rows.title: Rockaway Traditional Land
rows.summary: Rockaway preserves a Native name on the shores of a much older Lenape homeland. Bays, islands and waterways connected people before colonial deeds and settlement divided the land. Displacement did not end Lenape life: communities continue in the homeland and in nations beyond New York. Honoring Rockaway means connecting the familiar name to that living history, while treating particular family relationships with care.
rows.why_this_matters: Rockaway Traditional Land presents western Long Island, Jamaica Bay, Hempstead Bay, and the south shore islands as Native homeland. It connects early records with waterways, coastal movement, and the continued importance of public memory.

rows.title: Rockaway and the Southern Hempstead Bays
rows.summary: Rockaway people are described in older histories with a principal settlement near what is now Rockville Centre, with others spread through southern Hempstead and islands in the bays along the south shore. This places Native life around the waterways west of Merrick and Freeport as part of a connected regional world.
rows.address_label: Southern Hempstead bay landscape near Rockville Centre and Freeport
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Associated with Merrick Ancestral Land at its western edge, while also recognizing neighboring Rockaway Native geography.
rows.why_this_matters: The Rockaway and southern Hempstead bay landscape places Merrick history in relation to neighboring Native communities. Bays, islands, and waterways connected people across homelands before colonial town borders divided the map.

rows.title: Rockaway: Native Homeland, English Patent and Private Transfers
rows.summary: Rockaway was a Native coastal homeland before John Palmer’s 1685 deed and English governor Thomas Dongan’s patent. Follow the named parties, Hempstead’s competing claim and Palmer’s later transfer to Richard Cornell, without mistaking colonial title for Native disappearance.
rows.address_label: Rockaway Peninsula, Queens — regional historical context
rows.why_this_matters: Naming Palmer, Dongan, Cornell and the Native signers makes colonial land claims concrete. A recorded deed, an English patent and a later private transfer were different steps in asserting control; none is evidence that Native people or their relationships to the homeland disappeared.

rows.title: Ronkonkoma Moraine
rows.summary: Unkechaug, a name for the nation of Indigenous peoples living in Mastic, New York, translates to "people from beyond the hill." Today, these hills are part of the Ronkonkoma Moraine, a chain of hills that span the center of Long Island. The Unkechaug Nations territory once ran along the south of the Ronkonkoma Moraine.
rows.why_this_matters: The Ronkonkoma Moraine gives landscape context for the Unkechaug name and homeland. Donna Barron records Unkechaug as "People from Beyond the Hill," while John A. Strong places Unkechaug villages in the southern half of Brookhaven when Europeans arrived in the mid-seventeenth century. References: Donna Barron, The Long Island Indians and Their New England Ancestors; John A. Strong, The Unkechaug Indians of Eastern Long Island: A History (2011).

rows.title: Rugs
rows.summary: Rugs is recorded as a Southampton Town place-name at Noyack, connected with a neck of land and creek. The stream is associated with Thompson's Trout Ponds.
rows.address_label: General area of Trout Pond / Thompson's Trout Ponds, Noyack, Southampton Town

rows.title: Rugua Swamp
rows.summary: Rugua is recorded as a swamp in the Town of Babylon near Copiag Neck.

rows.title: Ruscocunks Creek
rows.summary: Ruscocunks is recorded as a creek east of Mastic Neck in the Town of Brookhaven.

rows.title: Ruskatux (Seaman's Neck)
rows.summary: A Seaford / Seaman's Neck placename for meadows and uplands east of an earlier Indian purchase.

rows.title: Sachem's Hole
rows.summary: Sachem's Hole, also known as Whooping Boy's Hollow and Buc-usk-kil, marks a resting place remembered in accounts of Poggatacut's funeral procession from Shelter Island toward Montauk.

rows.title: Sachem's House
rows.summary: Sachem's House connects a 1650 Southampton record with Shinnecock leadership and the way colonial documents sometimes preserved Native political places.

rows.title: Sachem's Neck
rows.summary: A Shelter Island placename connected to Native leadership, family movement, and Mashomuck history.

rows.title: Sackhickneyah Creek
rows.summary: Sackhickneyah is recorded as a creek in northern Newtown, Queens County, near Fish's Point.

rows.title: Sacut (Success Pond)
rows.summary: Sacut is recorded as the Native name for Success Pond at Lakeville in North Hempstead.
rows.address_label: Lake Success / Success Pond, Lake Success, NY (waterbody orientation)

rows.title: Sagamore Hill
rows.summary: William Wallace Tooker includes Sagamore Hill at Oyster Bay, recording Theodore Roosevelt's explanation that the name was a revival connected with local traditions about Mohannis Cove and Mohannis Hill.

rows.title: Sagaponack / Sagg Pond
rows.summary: Sagaponack is an eastern Southampton place-name also preserved in Sagg, Sagg Pond, and Sag Harbor. The name is connected with ground-nuts or Indian potatoes.

rows.title: Saghtekoos / Appletree Neck
rows.summary: Saghtekoos is recorded as a neck of land in Islip, known in English records as Appletree Neck.

rows.title: Santapogue Neck
rows.summary: Santapogue is recorded as a neck of land in Babylon, south of the settlement of Breslau, now Lindenhurst.

rows.title: Saphorackam
rows.summary: Saphorackam is recorded as a locality in southern Brooklyn, near the Long Island strand of the North River bay.

rows.title: Sassian's Maize Land
rows.summary: Sassians was a Brooklyn locality named in a 1642 Kieft grant as Sassian's maize land.

rows.title: Saugust Neck (Southold Old Field)
rows.summary: Saugust is recorded as a neck of land at the east part of Southold.

rows.title: Scoquams Creek / Schookwames Neck
rows.summary: Scoquams is recorded as a neck of land and small creek in Islip, east of Babylon village.

rows.title: Screcunkas (Cedar Island)
rows.summary: Screcunkas is recorded as an island in Great South Bay, now known as Cedar Island in Babylon.

rows.title: Scurraway / Josiah's Neck
rows.summary: Scurraway is recorded as the Native name of Josiah's Neck in Babylon, east of Amityville.

rows.title: Seabamuck / Sebamuck
rows.summary: Seabamuck is recorded as one of the lesser necks of the Manor of St. George at Mastic, first east of the Connecticut or Carmans River at its mouth.

rows.title: Seaford Creek and Unqua Neck Cultural Landscape
rows.summary: A south shore estuarine landscape tied to Native village life, shellfishing, fishing, bay travel, and coastal resource use in Merrick and Massapequa homelands.
rows.address_label: Seaford Creek / Unqua Neck waterways, Seaford-Massapequa area
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Within the wider Merrick/Massapequa south shore cultural landscape; linked here to Merrick Ancestral Land with care about overlapping homelands.
rows.why_this_matters: Seaford Creek and Unqua Neck show why tidal waterways and neck lands mattered: they were living landscapes, travel routes, and foodways rather than empty marshes.

rows.title: Seapoose (Meacox Bay Inlet)
rows.summary: Seapoose names inlets opened through the south-side beaches of East Hampton and Southampton, especially the inlet between Meacox Bay and the ocean.

rows.title: Seatquaa: Creek-Mouth Wetland Place Name
rows.summary: Seatquaa is a place-name connected with land at the mouth of a creek or tidal stream. The name helps explain how Native geographic language described estuaries, creek mouths, marshes, and movement through the south shore.
rows.address_label: South shore creek-mouth landscape, Freeport-Merrick-Bellmore area
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Linked to Merrick Ancestral Land as a south shore wetland/place-name learning point.
rows.why_this_matters: Seatquaa presents the south shore as Native geography: creek mouths, marshes, and bay edges were named and meaningful places for fishing, shellfishing, travel, and settlement. The word opens a way to understand wetlands as cultural landscapes.

rows.title: Seatuck Creek
rows.summary: Seatuck is a creek or river at Eastport on the boundary between Southampton and Brookhaven.
rows.address_label: Seatuck Creek, Eastport, NY (waterway orientation)

rows.title: Seawanhacky / Sewanhaka
rows.summary: Seawanhacky, also Sewanhaka, is a name for Long Island found in Dutch-period purchase documents.

rows.title: Sebonac Creek Settlement / Seponack
rows.summary: Seponack, also Sabonac, is recorded as a neck of land at Southampton on Peconic Bay. The name also connects the related Sebonac Creek Settlement and the Sabonack cross-reference.
rows.address_label: Sebonac Neck / Sebonac Road, Southampton, NY (broad public orientation)

rows.title: Secatogue Ancestral Land
rows.summary: Secatogue ancestry belongs to the creeks, meadows and shores of Great South Bay, where Native life long preceded colonial towns. Land transactions and settlement restricted that homeland and changed how its people appeared in written records. A less visible name is not evidence that a people vanished. This bay remains part of a living Native landscape, including neighboring Unkechaug and Shinnecock communities whose histories extend beyond reservation boundaries.
rows.why_this_matters: Secatogue Ancestral Land presents Great South Bay creeks, marshes, and inland routes as Native geography. It also connects older records to descendant community memory and the continued presence of Native families on Long Island.

rows.title: Secatogue Neck
rows.summary: Secatogue is recorded as a neck of land in Islip and the locality associated with the Secatogue people.
rows.address_label: Secatogue Neck / West Islip waterfront, West Islip, NY (broad public orientation)

rows.title: Secatogues
rows.summary: Secatogue is used in older sources for a south-shore Native community and place-name region east of Massapequa. Its history belongs with tidal creeks, Great South Bay travel, fishing and shellfish places, kinship, neighboring communities, regional diplomacy, and colonial land pressure.

rows.title: Senex Creek / Senekes River
rows.summary: Senex is recorded as a creek at Center Moriches, also called Senekes River or Creek.
rows.address_label: Senix Creek, Center Moriches, NY (waterway orientation)
rows.activity_update_summary: Moved the 1693 survey detail into the cited Historic Moment and removed the repeated history paragraph.

rows.title: Setalcott Powwow Grounds
rows.summary: The Setalcott Corn Festival Pow-Wow brings Native community members and visitors together at Setauket Elementary School for cultural education and celebration. Dates vary by year; attend only during announced public events.
rows.listing_image_alt: Setaukett Setalcott Powwow Grounds School5I5A0306 WEB

rows.title: Setauket Ancestral Land
rows.summary: Setauket carries a Native place name within the living homeland of the Setalcott Nation. Its history reaches back thousands of years and continues through descendant families, including the Black and Indigenous community around Christian Avenue. Colonial land taking and later exclusion did not erase those ties. Setalcott people continue to share community history and shape how their homeland is remembered and cared for today.
rows.why_this_matters: Setauket Ancestral Land presents the north-central shore as Native homeland, not only as colonial-settlement history. It connects language, villages, land records, descendant community memory, and contemporary cultural education.

rows.title: Sexton Island: Native Coastal Homeland, Colonial Claims and Municipal Leases
rows.summary: Sexton Island is part of a living Native coastal homeland. Colonial patents, a national seashore boundary and municipal leases record different claims to control; none by itself establishes when Native rights to this island were surrendered.
rows.address_label: Sexton Island, Great South Bay — modern island context
rows.why_this_matters: A government grant, park boundary and lease are not interchangeable. Their differences help explain how control of a Native coastal homeland became organized through colonial and municipal property systems without implying that Native people disappeared.

rows.title: Shagwong Point, Hill, and Reef
rows.summary: Shagwong is a Montauk placename for a hill, point of land, and reef on the northeastern part of the peninsula, within the Indian Fields area.

rows.title: Shahchippitchage Boundary Stones
rows.summary: Shahchippitchage is a Montauk boundary-mark name for a pile of stones in North Neck, in the land between Fort Pond and Lake Montauk.

rows.title: Shanscomacocke (Flatlands)
rows.summary: Shanscomacocke is a Kings County placename at Flatlands, associated with enclosed upland, marsh, and beach land near the ocean.

rows.title: Shelter Island Plantation Claim (1651–1652)
rows.summary: On Manhansett homeland between Long Island’s forks, Nathaniel and Constant Sylvester, Thomas Middleton and Thomas Rouse claimed an island-wide plantation supplying Barbados. Native residents challenged threatened removal. The story connects contested land agreements, Native labor, African enslavement and continuing Indigenous relationships.
rows.address_label: Approximate historical landscape — not a visitor entrance
rows.why_this_matters: A colonial land record describes a claim made at a particular time. Read its conditions and the people affected alongside the map; an outlined claim is not proof that Native relationships or rights ended.

rows.title: Sherawoug (Stony Brook Harbor)
rows.summary: Sherawoug is recorded as a locality on the east side of Stony Brook Harbor, near St. James in Smithtown.

rows.title: Shinnecock Ancestral Land
rows.summary: Shinnecock people have belonged to this Southampton homeland since time immemorial. Shinnecock Bay, the Hills and Canoe Place connect ancestral life with a living nation. Colonial land loss and later development reduced access to this much larger homeland; they did not end Shinnecock belonging. Today the Shinnecock Indian Nation sustains self-government, family and cultural life, with community on and beyond the reservation and continuing ties to Westwoods.
rows.activity_update_summary: Consolidated the Shinnecock place-name history, preserved its citations, and clarified two separately attributed name interpretations.
rows.why_this_matters: Shinnecock Ancestral Land presents Southampton and the South Fork as the homeland of a living Native nation. It connects early records, Native leadership, land protection, cultural continuity, and present-day Shinnecock sovereignty.

rows.title: Shinnecock Hills
rows.summary: Shinnecock Hills is sacred Shinnecock land and a burial landscape with ancestors present for thousands of years. The hills also sit at the center of later land-loss history, preservation fights, and public disputes over development, golf, and recognition of Shinnecock land rights.
rows.address_label: Sunrise Highway / Shinnecock Territory, Southampton
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Shinnecock Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Shinnecock Hills Golf Club
rows.summary: Shinnecock Hills Golf Club sits within the broader Shinnecock Hills landscape, part of Shinnecock ancestral territory and the land at the center of the 1703 lease and 1859 land-loss history. The course is also a place where Shinnecock labor, caddying, greenskeeping, and golf history are visible, including Oscar Bunn and generations of Shinnecock workers. The 2026 U.S. Open brings global attention back to this landscape, making source-grounded land acknowledgment especially important.
rows.address_label: Shinnecock Hills Golf Club, Southampton, NY (general public course area)
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shinnecock Hills is documented in Shinnecock land-history sources as part of the lands covered by the 1703 lease and later 1859 land-loss dispute. The marker gives broad course-area context rather than a burial or other sensitive-site coordinate.
rows.why_this_matters: The 2026 U.S. Open landscape is Shinnecock homeland, not only a famous golf course. It connects championship history to land loss, burial-ground disruption, and Shinnecock labor and skill: tribal members helped build and maintain the course, Oscar Bunn played in the 1896 U.S. Open, and later Shinnecock workers shaped the grounds across generations.

rows.title: Shinnecock Indian Reservation
rows.summary: The Shinnecock Reservation is a continuing Shinnecock homeland and center of Shinnecock government, culture, family life, education, worship, art, shellfish restoration, and community gathering. More than a historic district, it is a living Native nation space tied to Shinnecock land defense, the annual powwow, cultural preservation, and ongoing sovereignty.
rows.address_label: 1 Church St, Southampton, NY 11968
rows.activity_update_summary: Rewrote the name discussion in public-facing language and preserved the Tooker and Goddard interpretations with clear attribution.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Shinnecock Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Shinnecock Monument
rows.summary: The Shinnecock Monument is an economic development project launched in early May 2019. The Shinnecock Nation's goal with this project is to generate revenue to provide for its people. Being a sovereign nation, The Shinnecock Nation maintains the right to build on its land and pursue commerce free from civil regulatory restrictions improperly imposed by New York State.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added respectful visiting guidance with a concise answer, context, and source references.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Shinnecock Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Shinnecock Nation Cultural Center and Museum
rows.summary: The Shinnecock Nation Cultural Center and Museum is a Shinnecock-owned and operated museum dedicated to Shinnecock and Eastern Woodland history, culture, art, and living community memory. The museum preserves and interprets materials connected to Shinnecock life while challenging older museum habits that treated Native people as figures of the past.
rows.activity_update_summary: Consolidated the existing dated chronology into cited Historic Moments and removed the duplicate unformatted history block.

rows.title: Shinnecock Outpost Tax Demonstrations
rows.summary: The Shinnecock Outpost became a public assertion of Shinnecock sovereignty during 1997 organizing against renewed state tax pressure.
rows.address_label: Shinnecock Indian Outpost, 42 Montauk Highway, Southampton, NY 11968
rows.why_this_matters: This stop connects local Shinnecock action to wider Native coalitions across New York.

rows.title: Shinnecock Oyster Project
rows.summary: The Shinnecock Oyster Project connects Shinnecock maritime knowledge, shellfish restoration, aquaculture training, environmental stewardship, and living Native continuity in Shinnecock Bay.

rows.title: Shinnecock Powwow Grounds
rows.summary: Formally organized in 1946, the Shinnecock Powwow is a decades long traditional and cultural celebration that takes place on the Shinnecock Indian Reservation. Every year on Labor Day weekend, the Powwow takes place on Shinnecock and is open to the public. The annual four-day Shinnecock Labor Day Powwow attracts more than 15,000 attendees each day and serves as both a cultural focal point and fundraiser for the Nation. The Powwow began as historical 'pageants' that took place throughout Southampton Town,.
rows.activity_pin_preview: The Shinnecock Nation hosts the 80th Annual Shinnecock Powwow on Labor Day Weekend, September 4-7, 2026, at the Shinnecock Powwow Grounds, 100 Montauk Hwy, Southampton. Source: Shinnecock Nation annual powwow page.
rows.activity_update_summary: Kept Hunter's disputed 1936 fundraiser account in the cited Historic Timeline and removed the duplicate article section.

rows.title: Shinnecock Presbyterian Church
rows.summary: The Shinnecock Presbyterian church on the Shinnecock Indian Reservation has been described as “the oldest, ongoing Native American church in America.” A regular schedule of tribal gatherings occur here, including the annual June Meeting, Indian Thanksgiving dinner and harvest celebrations. For many years, tribal meetings and Tribal Council elections were held in the Parish Hall before taking place in the Tribal Community Center. The Shinnecock Powwow was first organized by the Presbyterian church congregation as a.
rows.activity_update_summary: Consolidated the church history into the cited Historic Timeline, preserving its photographs, community context, Ogburn history, and disputed 1936 fundraiser account without duplicate sections.

rows.title: Shockheyoune
rows.summary: Shockheyoune appears in deed language for a swamp and creek at the Nissequogue River mouth. Its location on the west side of the river connects the name to shoreline, wetland, and boundary records along Long Island Sound.
rows.address_label: West side of the Nissequogue River mouth, Kings Park, NY (broad wetland orientation)
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Nissequogue Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Sintsinck (Manhasset Bay)
rows.summary: Sintsinck was recorded for Manhasset Bay or a locality on the bay at Cow Neck, with a separate related use recorded near Hell Gate Neck in Queens.

rows.title: Skow Island (South Oyster Bay)
rows.summary: Skow Island is a tidal marsh island in South Oyster Bay. Tooker recorded Skow as an early-map spelling associated with the island; modern federal maps preserve the island at this exact location under an outdated historical name.
rows.address_label: South Oyster Bay marsh island, Nassau County, NY
rows.why_this_matters: The island is a clearly identifiable part of the South Oyster Bay marsh landscape. Mapping it with careful language allows the archive to preserve a historical place-name record without repeating outdated terminology as an unqualified public label.

rows.title: Skupash Creek (Jamaica Meadows)
rows.summary: A Jamaica Meadows creek name recorded in a 1657 division of meadow lots.

rows.title: Slongo / Sunken Meadow
rows.summary: Slongo is a recorded name associated with Sunk Meadow, now Sunken Meadow, in Smithtown. Its location is clear, but its linguistic origin remains unresolved and may not be Indigenous.
rows.address_label: Sunken Meadow Creek, Sunken Meadow State Park, Kings Park, NY
rows.activity_update_summary: Removed a short introduction that repeated the listing summary.
rows.why_this_matters: Slongo is useful precisely because the map can separate a confident location from an uncertain origin. Publishing the record with that distinction prevents a historical name from being presented as confirmed Indigenous language when the available sources do not establish that conclusion.

rows.title: Smithtown: Contested Land and Native Rights
rows.summary: Nissequogue people challenged Richard Smith’s claim to their land. Agreements recorded payments and retained rights; colonial patents then strengthened an inheritable estate and required English settlement.
rows.address_label: Approximate historical landscape — not a visitor entrance
rows.why_this_matters: Land loss was a process involving agreements, contested claims, colonial institutions and restrictions on Native access. Read the actors, obligations and continuing communities together; a broad outline does not mean every Native right ended on one date.

rows.title: Sonquoequahesick / Sonnquoquas
rows.summary: Sonquoequahesick, also Sonnquoquas, is associated with Sonquoqua and Tom's Creek on Hashamomuk Neck in Southold.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Corchaug Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: South Harbor
rows.summary: South Harbor and Indian Neck are connected to Corchaug homelands and a contested record of Native land in Southold. Later sources describe Southold setting aside a 120- or 125-acre tract at South Harbor in 1685. Corchaug family tradition says families were pushed from that tract around 1690, while a 1763 petition stated that Corchaug descendants had lived at Indian Neck since 1691 and had never settled at South Harbor.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added pre-1685 Corchaug land-pressure context, carefully attributed family tradition about South Harbor, the 1763 Indian Neck petition, and expanded source connections.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Corchaug Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
rows.why_this_matters: The 1763 petition preserves Corchaug descendants' own challenge to a land history written largely through Southold's records. Their statement of continued residence at Indian Neck rejects the idea that Native families simply disappeared or abandoned the North Fork. Read alongside the 1685 record and later family tradition, it makes this a history of continuing presence, memory, and legal resistance—not only a colonial allotment.

rows.title: South Ocean Gallery at South Nassau Unitarian Universalist Congregation
rows.summary: South Ocean Gallery at South Nassau Unitarian Universalist Congregation in Freeport is the venue for Living Conduit - Indigenous History and Present Day, a fall 2026 exhibition by Shinnecock artist Jeremy Dennis.
rows.address_label: 228 South Ocean Avenue, Freeport, NY 11520
rows.listing_image_alt: South Nassau Unitarian Universalist Congregation in Freeport, home of South Ocean Gallery. Photograph © Jeremy Dennis, September 12, 2026.
rows.why_this_matters: This Freeport venue is part of the modern acknowledgment landscape for Merrick/Freeport-area Indigenous history. The 2026 Living Conduit exhibition connects On This Site place research with contemporary Shinnecock portraiture, education, and continuing Long Island Indigenous presence.

rows.title: South Street Seaport Museum
rows.summary: The Seaport Museum holds two photographs from Jeremy Dennis’s On This Site. Circassian Site recalls the ten Shinnecock people who drowned in 1876 helping the crew of the wrecked ship Circassian off Mecox Bay.
rows.address_label: 12 Fulton Street, New York, NY 10038
rows.listing_image_alt: Circassian Site (2017) by Jeremy Dennis, from On This Site. The South Street Seaport Museum holds a print.
rows.why_this_matters: The 1876 wreck of the Circassian is part of the history of New York shipping, and so are the ten Shinnecock people who drowned helping its crew. With this photograph in its collection, a maritime museum keeps their part in that story.

rows.title: Southold Indian Museum
rows.summary: The Southold Indian Museum opened its public museum building in 1962 under the Long Island Chapter of the New York State Archaeological Association. Its collections history includes a pivotal 1990 challenge by Shinnecock community members to the display of ancestral human remains.
rows.address_label: 1080 Main Bayview Rd, Southold, NY 11971
rows.activity_update_summary: Restored the article's Alix Biel photograph of David Bunn Martine and John A. Strong and strengthened the public summary of the museum's 1990 remains-display and repatriation history.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Corchaug Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
rows.why_this_matters: The museum's history raises questions about who has authority over Native ancestors and collections. In 1990, Shinnecock artist David Bunn Martine, historian John A. Strong, and other community members called for human remains on display to be respectfully removed. The museum covered and dismantled the display while its board considered their return for proper burial, marking an important shift toward consultation and repatriation.

rows.title: Souwassett (Port Jefferson)
rows.summary: Souwassett is a locality at Port Jefferson in Brookhaven, connected with the earlier English name Drowned Meadow.

rows.title: Speonk (Neck, River, and Village)
rows.summary: A Native name for the Speonk neck, river and village landscape; its precise translation remains uncertain.

rows.title: Springy Banks Pow Wow Grounds
rows.summary: Springy Banks at Three Mile Harbor became an intertribal gathering place for powwows in 1944 and 1945, with later gatherings continuing into the early 1950s. Montaukett, Shinnecock, Matinecock, Narragansett, Schaghticoke, Cherokee, and other Native participants met there.
rows.address_label: Springy Banks / Three Mile Harbor, East Hampton (generalized)
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Montaukett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
rows.why_this_matters: The Springy Banks gatherings show Native people building regional relationships during the mid-twentieth century, when public histories often spoke of Long Island's Indigenous communities only in the past. The powwows affirmed community, diplomacy, and continuing Native presence.

rows.title: Squam-Pit Purchase
rows.summary: Squam-Pit is recorded as a tract near Deer Park, now in the Wyandanch area, historically within Huntington.

rows.title: Squassux Landing / Squassucks Point
rows.summary: Squassux Landing / Squassucks Point is a Carmans River mouth placename tied to Unkechaug history, clay beds, pottery, ferry landings, and local memory at Brookhaven.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Unkechaug Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: St. Matthew Chapel
rows.summary: St. Matthew Chapel is one of the surviving buildings associated with Freetown, an East Hampton neighborhood shaped by Black and Montaukett families. Built in 1852, the chapel served local worshippers before it was moved to the Maidstone Marina boatyard in 1976.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Montaukett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Stephen Talkhouse Pharoah House
rows.summary: The Stephen Talkhouse Pharoah house was used by Pharoah later in his life. The house featured two "Indian barns" as food storage, and a footpath toward Bridgehampton on it's edge. The foundation remains today, but the house may have been a wood cabin during its use.
rows.address_label: Old Tar Road area
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Montaukett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Stony Brook Site
rows.summary: The Stony Brook Site is an archaeological site in Stony Brook, New York, connected with Archaic-period Native occupation near the North Shore area of Aunt Amy's Creek. Excavations by William A. Ritchie and later archaeologists helped document long Indigenous presence, toolmaking, shellfish use, and the need to protect archaeological places from disturbance.
rows.activity_update_summary: Consolidated the dated Stony Brook research into cited Historic Moments and moved its stewardship questions into a clearly formatted learning section.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Setauket Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Stony Brook University
rows.summary: Stony Brook University stands on the territory the university identifies as Wopowog, connected to the Setalcott people. Its campus relationships include Algonquian language revitalization, an Indigenous language and art exhibition, Native American and Indigenous Studies, and support for Native students.
rows.address_label: 100 Nicolls Road, Stony Brook, NY 11794
rows.why_this_matters: Stony Brook is a living Long Island example of Indigenous language revitalization, Native-led and Native-connected scholarship, public art, and student support taking place on Setalcott territory.

rows.title: Sucos (Brookville)
rows.summary: Sucos is recorded as the site of Brookville in Oyster Bay, historically remembered as Suco's wigwam.

rows.title: Sugar Loaf Hill
rows.summary: Sugar Loaf Hill is tied to Orient-period burial context in the Shinnecock Hills and decades of Shinnecock advocacy for burial protection. Historic maps and later preservation efforts show how burial landscapes have been marked, damaged, contested, and defended.
rows.address_label: Montauk Highway corridor
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Shinnecock Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Suggamuck (Birch Creek)
rows.summary: Suggamuck is recorded as a creek near Flanders, now called Birch Creek, one of the creeks at the west end of Peconic Bay.

rows.title: Sumpawams Creek and Neck
rows.summary: Sumpawams is a Babylon-area name now applied to the creek between Babylon and Islip, originally belonging to the neck where much of Babylon village stands.

rows.title: Sungic (Shelter Island)
rows.summary: Sungic is a point of land and creek on the east side of Shelter Island, facing Gardiners Bay.

rows.title: Sunkapogue Creek (Mastic Neck)
rows.summary: Sunkapogue is a creek in Brookhaven on Mastic Neck, connected with the east bounds of a half-neck of land.

rows.title: Sunwicks Creek (Astoria)
rows.summary: Sunwicks is a creek at Astoria in Queens, near Hell Gate on Long Island.

rows.title: Swego / Centerport
rows.summary: Swego is a Huntington locality recorded in a 1771 town order. A Town of Huntington historical marker identifies the name with this Centerport area on Fort Salonga Road.
rows.address_label: Fort Salonga Road near Stony Hollow Road, Centerport, NY
rows.why_this_matters: The surviving town marker turns Swego from a broad Huntington reference into a mappable Centerport locality. The listing also shows how a location can be secure even when competing historical interpretations of a name remain unsettled.

rows.title: Sylvester Manor
rows.summary: Sylvester Manor stands on Manchonack / Shelter Island, a Manhansett homeland later transformed into a colonial provisioning plantation tied to Barbados commerce, enslavement, indenture, and Indigenous dispossession. In 1829, Montaukett brothers William and Isaac Pharoah, ages eight and five, were indentured there until age twenty-one. William escaped in 1840 and joined a New London whaling voyage; Isaac completed his indenture and remained at the Manor.
rows.activity_update_summary: Consolidated the existing dated chronology into cited Historic Moments and removed the duplicate unformatted history block.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Manhansett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
rows.why_this_matters: William and Isaac Pharoah place Montaukett childhood, labor, resistance, maritime skill, and continuity at the center of Sylvester Manor's history. Their lives belong beside the histories of Manhansett homeland, enslaved African labor, Barbados commerce, and colonial dispossession that shaped the Manor landscape.

rows.title: Syosset
rows.summary: Syosset is a documented village name in Oyster Bay, but the available historical interpretation derives it through the Dutch word schout rather than from a Native landscape term.
rows.address_label: Syosset, Town of Oyster Bay, NY
rows.why_this_matters: Not every Long Island name that sounds Indigenous has a confirmed Indigenous origin. Syosset provides a visible correction and demonstrates why language claims should be checked against records instead of repeated from appearance alone.

rows.title: Tackan
rows.summary: Tackan is recorded as a tract of land in Smithtown on the Nissequogue River.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Setauket Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Tackapausha Museum and Preserve
rows.summary: A Seaford nature preserve bears the name of Tackapousha, a Massapequa sachem whose diplomacy shaped seventeenth-century Long Island. Its museum and trails connect that remembered name with the south shore’s living habitats.
rows.address_label: Tackapausha Museum, 2225 Washington Avenue, Seaford, NY 11783
rows.why_this_matters: Tackapousha’s name connects a familiar nature preserve with a Native leader who negotiated for his community. Learning that history while exploring the preserve brings political leadership and care for the living landscape into the same view.

rows.title: Tatamuckatakis (Great Neck Creek)
rows.summary: Tatamuckatakis is recorded as a neck and creek in Babylon, west of Copiague Neck, now known as Great Neck and Great Neck Creek.

rows.title: Tatamuckatakis / Yatamuntitahege
rows.summary: Yatamuntitahege is treated as a cross-reference to Tatamuckatakis. The related name is tied to a river bounding Copiag Neck in the western part of Babylon.

rows.title: Taukoms (Lacten's Neck)
rows.summary: A Babylon neck placename that preserves Native and English naming layers in the same landscape.

rows.title: Tenkenas (Ward's Island)
rows.summary: Tenkenas was the Native name recorded for Ward's Island in the East River, formerly also called Great Barcut or Great Barn Island.

rows.title: Tersarge / Crab Meadow
rows.summary: Tersarge is a seventeenth-century locality on Long Island's north shore. Later historical research connects the name with the Crab Meadow landscape east of Huntington.
rows.address_label: Crab Meadow Wetlands and Beach, Northport, NY (general area)
rows.activity_update_summary: Removed a short introduction that repeated the listing summary.
rows.why_this_matters: Tersarge ties a surviving Native place name to a documented claim of kinship and inheritance on the north shore. Placing it broadly at Crab Meadow makes the history visible while avoiding a false claim that the seventeenth-century allotment boundary has been precisely reconstructed.

rows.title: The Heckscher Museum of Art
rows.summary: Home to Jeremy Dennis’s Weeckatuck from On This Site. Explore Native landscape photography, Shinnecock art, and Eclipse of the Sun Now, September 26, 2026–May 9, 2027.
rows.address_label: 2 Prime Avenue, Huntington, NY 11743
rows.listing_image_alt: Artwork by Jeremy Dennis: Weeckatuck (2016), archival inkjet print, 13 × 19 inches. The Heckscher Museum of Art, Gift of the Artists and Ignivomous Inc. Accession 2022.6.12.
rows.why_this_matters: The woodland path in Weeckatuck holds a history that a scenic view alone cannot tell. Jeremy Dennis’s photograph brings the memory of a Shinnecock community into the museum, while Courtney M. Leonard’s porcelain map connects Long Island’s shape with the touch of a maker’s hand. These works invite visitors to see a landscape through the people, names, and relationships it carries.

rows.title: The Point
rows.summary: The Point is a Shinnecock Reservation marshland remembered through community use for fishing, hunting, gathering, and teaching across generations. The listing speaks from local Shinnecock landscape knowledge and does not direct readers to sensitive areas.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Shinnecock Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: The Stephen Talkhouse
rows.summary: The Amagansett music venue carries the name of Stephen Talkhouse Pharoah, a Montaukett whaler, Civil War veteran and famous walker who died in 1879. Jeremy Dennis’s On This Site photograph of his house site is on view there.
rows.address_label: 161 Main Street, Amagansett, NY 11930
rows.listing_image_alt: The site of Stephen Talkhouse Pharoah’s house, photographed by Jeremy Dennis for On This Site.
rows.why_this_matters: Many people know the Talkhouse as a music venue without knowing whose name it carries. The photograph on view there leads back to Stephen Talkhouse Pharoah’s home and to the Montaukett history behind the name.

rows.title: The Watermill Center
rows.summary: The Watermill Center is an arts residency, archive, and research library on Shinnecock ancestral territory. Jeremy Dennis developed On This Site there during a June 2017 residency, and Watermill has worked with Shinnecock artists, cultural workers, and staff including Shane Weeks, Andrina Smith, Denise Silva-Dennis, and Kelly Dennis.
rows.address_label: 39 Water Mill Towd Road, Water Mill, NY 11976
rows.listing_image_alt: On This Site, Edition 2, displayed in The Watermill Center research library
rows.ancestral_territory_note: The Watermill Center identifies its ten-acre campus as Shinnecock ancestral territory.
rows.why_this_matters: The Watermill Center connects On This Site's digital map to the residency where its book and exhibition took shape. It also documents sustained Shinnecock artistic labor, administration, education, and collaboration at an institution that identifies its campus as Shinnecock ancestral territory.

rows.title: Three Village Historical Society and Museum
rows.summary: A public museum and archive in East Setauket preserving local history, including Setalcott oral histories and community records.
rows.address_label: 93 North Country Road, East Setauket, NY
rows.why_this_matters: Listening to local people changes how a place is understood. This museum offers a way to encounter Setalcott community memory alongside the colonial records that often dominate accounts of the North Shore.

rows.title: Tianna / Tiana Bay and Creek
rows.summary: Tianna is a bay and creek name at Good Ground, now Hampton Bays, in western Southampton.
rows.address_label: Tiana Bay, Hampton Bays, NY

rows.title: Tinnie's Water Hole / Napeague Beach
rows.summary: In his 1911 place-name study, William Wallace Tooker recorded Tinnie's as a water hole on Napeague Beach near the Amagansett Hills. The historic water hole has not been matched to a named modern pond, so this marker represents the broader Napeague beach and dune landscape.
rows.address_label: Napeague State Park, East Hampton, NY (broad representative point)
rows.why_this_matters: The name records a small water feature within the Napeague coastal landscape and a story about a woman whose identity was not preserved in the printed account. A broad marker keeps the record searchable without inventing an exact pond or treating an unverified story as established fact.

rows.title: Towapionke (John Wood's Neck)
rows.summary: Towapionke is a tract east of Mastic Neck in Brookhaven, later known as John Wood's Neck.

rows.title: Towd (North Sea Wading Place)
rows.summary: Towd is a locality near North Sea in Southampton, described as a cove above a wading place.

rows.title: Toyonge (Red Creek)
rows.summary: Toyonge is Red Creek at the head of Peconic Bay in Southampton.
rows.address_label: Red Creek area, Southampton, NY

rows.title: Tuckahoe (Southampton)
rows.summary: Tuckahoe is a level tract of land and school district north of Southampton Village.

rows.title: Tuckahoe Gate Hill / Shinnecock Hills
rows.summary: Tuckahoe Gate Hill is Tooker's reference to one hill in the Shinnecock Hills range near the historic Tuckahoe gate. The marker represents the broader documented hill landscape rather than claiming an exact summit.
rows.address_label: General Tuckahoe Road / Shinnecock Hills area, Southampton, NY (approximate)
rows.why_this_matters: A broad marker keeps this recorded Shinnecock Hills place visible without assigning Tooker's historical label to a private parcel or pretending that the precise hill has been recovered.

rows.title: Turkom (Menantic Neck)
rows.summary: Turkom is a small point or neck between two creeks near Menantic Neck on Shelter Island.

rows.title: Uncawamuck (Reeve's Creek)
rows.summary: Uncawamuck is a creek placename near Mattituck, associated with a canoe portage and the Ocquebauck land-title landscape.

rows.title: Unkawa Neck / Unqua Creek
rows.summary: Unkawa was a neck-place name on the Babylon and Oyster Bay town boundary, connected with the later Unqua stream name.

rows.title: Unkechaug Ancestral Land
rows.summary: Unkechaug people continue to live in their ancestral South Shore homeland at Poospatuck, where the creek leads toward the Forge River and Moriches Bay. Generations of fishing, family life and care for the waters connect this reservation community to a much wider homeland. Despite colonial dispossession and continuing pressure on their land, the Unkechaug Indian Nation sustains its government, community and work to renew its language.
rows.why_this_matters: Unkechaug Ancestral Land connects Poospatuck and the south shore Brookhaven landscape with a living Native homeland. Land, water, language, governance, and community continuity run from early records to the present.

rows.title: Unkechaug Indian Reservation
rows.summary: The Unkechaug Indian Nation is a Native nation recognized by New York State and centered on the Poospatuck Reservation along Poospatuck Creek in Mastic. The reservation is a continuing homeland where Unkechaug people maintain government, community, language work, and relationships with land and water.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Unkechaug Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
rows.why_this_matters: Poospatuck is a living Unkechaug homeland and seat of government, not a remnant of a disappeared people. Its history connects land defense, state law, family continuity, language revitalization, and present-day Native sovereignty on Long Island.

rows.title: Van Cortlandt Park — Stockbridge Memorial
rows.summary: At Indian Field, the Chief Nimham Memorial remembers Native soldiers killed fighting for the American cause on August 31, 1778. David Bunn Martine’s painting connects that history with possible Shinnecock and Montaukett participation.
rows.address_label: Chief Nimham Memorial, Van Cortlandt Park East near East 238th Street / Oneida Avenue, Bronx, NY
rows.why_this_matters: The memorial connects the American Revolution to Native soldiers whose families also fought to hold on to their homelands. David Bunn Martine’s painting carries this remembrance into Long Island’s contemporary Native art, inviting attention to people whose individual stories are still being recovered.

rows.title: Wading River Site
rows.summary: The Wading River Site is the oldest clearly-dated archaic period village site located near the mouth of the Wading River, an ideal place to draw food resources from the freshwater stream and Long Island sound. It's sheltered location protected the villagers from the cold north and western winds, signifying its use in the winter, while abundant shellfish remains show spring and summer occupation; thus the site was used year-round. This camp, according to Ritchie who studied the site in 1955-56, was part of a.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Setauket Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Wagaspor (Flatlands Meadows)
rows.summary: Wagaspor is a creek in the Flatlands meadows of Kings County.

rows.title: Wallage / Old Westbury
rows.summary: Wallage is a historical name associated with the Westbury settlement in North Hempstead. Later place histories consistently connect the older locality with the area now known as Old Westbury.
rows.address_label: Old Westbury, Nassau County, NY (representative point)
rows.why_this_matters: Wallage preserves an older layer beneath the names Woodedge, Westbury, and Old Westbury. Mapping the name broadly makes that sequence visible while acknowledging the disagreement in older printed sources.

rows.title: Wampmissic
rows.summary: Wampmissic is a tract of land and large swamp in Brookhaven, between Yaphank and Manor stations on the Long Island Rail Road. The name is interpreted as a place of chestnut trees.

rows.title: Wamponamon (Montauk Point)
rows.summary: Wamponamon is the extreme eastern end of Long Island at Montauk Point, where the lighthouse stands.

rows.title: Wanasquattan (Amityville)
rows.summary: A western Babylon placename near Amityville connected with Massapequa proprietors and a 1696 Huntington grant.

rows.title: Wandowenock (Newtown)
rows.summary: Wandowenock was reported as a name for the eastern portion of Newtown in Queens, with meaning unresolved.

rows.title: Wantagh
rows.summary: Wantagh is connected to recorded forms related to Wiandance or Wyandanch, the Montaukett grand sachem whose name appears widely in Long Island Native history. The modern village adopted Wantagh as a public place name in 1891.
rows.address_label: Wantagh village area
rows.listing_image_alt: The Wantagh historical marker. Its inscription reflects the marker’s historical interpretation of the place name. Photograph © Jeremy Dennis, September 12, 2026.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Wantagh’s history connects Merrick, Massapequa, and Montaukett communities.
rows.why_this_matters: Wantagh shows how Native names continue to shape public geography, even when modern usage is separated from the original communities, languages, and political histories. A familiar place name can remember Native presence while leaving important histories unexplained.

rows.title: Wantagh High School: Indigenous Mascot Debate
rows.summary: Wantagh’s ongoing Warrior-name dispute connects school identity with Native calls for respectful representation. In February 2026, the district announced a compliance extension to June 2027.
rows.address_label: Wantagh High School, 3297 Beltagh Avenue, Wantagh, NY
rows.listing_image_alt: Wantagh High School signage displaying “Home of the Warriors” and a Native-head mascot, photographed September 12, 2026. Photograph © Jeremy Dennis, September 12, 2026.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Contemporary Indigenous representation in the Merrick–Wantagh area.
rows.why_this_matters: A student newspaper’s disagreement over the Wantagh mascot brings Indigenous representation into an everyday public institution. Reading that debate alongside Native Nations’ recorded support for change connects school traditions with the people those traditions claim to represent.

rows.title: Wantagh Naming Marker
rows.summary: A 1936 roadside sign at the Wantagh Museum commemorates the Native leader remembered in the community’s name.
rows.address_label: Wantagh Museum grounds, Wantagh Avenue and Emeric Avenue
rows.listing_image_alt: The Wantagh historical marker. Its inscription reflects the marker’s historical interpretation of the place name. Photograph © Jeremy Dennis, September 12, 2026.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: The Wantagh name recalls Montaukett leadership within the wider history of western Long Island.
rows.why_this_matters: Everyday place names can lead to histories that a brief roadside sign only begins to tell. Wantagh’s marker offers a starting point for learning about Native leaders and how later communities chose to remember them.

rows.title: Warrasketuck Creek
rows.summary: Warrasketuck is a creek at Amityville on the boundary between South Oyster Bay and Babylon. The name is interpreted as the ending or point creek.

rows.title: Warratta Neck
rows.summary: Warratta is a neck of land at Center Moriches between Barnes mill-pond on Terrell River and Senex Creek.

rows.title: Watchogue
rows.summary: An East Moriches neck placename, with a related Islip use west of Bay Shore.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Unkechaug Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Wattuquasset (Lake Montauk)
rows.summary: Wattuquasset is a small neck on the southwest side of Great Pond at Montauk, now Lake Montauk.

rows.title: Waubheag (Rockaway Neck)
rows.summary: Waubheag preserves a Rockaway Neck waterway name in Queens. The name belongs to broad place-name and boundary-record context within the Rockaway and Jamaica Bay landscape.

rows.title: Wauwepex (Cold Spring Harbor)
rows.summary: Wauwepex is the reported Native name for the original settlement on the west side of Cold Spring Harbor. The name is interpreted as a good little water-place.

rows.title: Weckatuck (Neck and Spring)
rows.summary: Weckatuck is a neck and spring placename near the foot of Long Beach by Noyack Road, associated with a nearby Native village and shell-heap site.
rows.activity_update_summary: Removed a second description that repeated the same Weckatuck location text.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Shinnecock Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Weekewackmamish (Mill Creek)
rows.summary: Weekewackmamish is Mill Creek at Southport in Southampton, emptying into Peconic Bay.
rows.address_label: Mill Creek at Noyack, Southampton, NY (waterway orientation)

rows.title: Weesuck
rows.summary: Weesuck is the clearer modern form of the longer placename Achabachawesuck. It refers to a small creek or brook between Fourth Neck and Pine Neck in what was historically Atlanticville, now the East Quogue area of Southampton.
rows.address_label: Weesuck Creek, East Quogue, NY

rows.title: Wegwagonock
rows.summary: Wegwagonock was once a large settlement in what is now the northern shore of Sag Harbor town. In around 1846, the ground containing burials and evidence of a Native village site were destroyed and used as stability material for the ship and oil yards.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Shinnecock Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Werpos
rows.summary: A Brooklyn placename near Merechkawikingh, recorded in a 1640 Kieft patent and interpreted as a bushy place or thicket.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Canarsie Traditional Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Wertheim National Wildlife Refuge
rows.summary: Wertheim National Wildlife Refuge protects habitat along the Carmans River in Shirley and houses the Long Island National Wildlife Refuge Complex visitor center. Inside, an interpretive section shares Unkechaug Nation history and displays objects connected with that history. At the center's November 2011 dedication, representatives of the Unkechaug and Shinnecock Nations offered a traditional blessing, recognizing enduring Native relationships with the river, wetlands, and wildlife.
rows.why_this_matters: Wertheim is not only a protected river and wetland landscape. Its visitor center makes Unkechaug Nation history visible to the public, while the 2011 blessing by Unkechaug and Shinnecock representatives recognized continuing Native relationships with the Carmans River, wetlands, and wildlife.

rows.title: West Fire Island: Native Coastal Homeland, Private Parcels and Federal Ownership
rows.summary: West Fire Island belongs to a living Native coastal homeland. Records of company parcels and federal acquisition show later control of the island; public conservation ownership is not the same as returning Indigenous land or jurisdiction.
rows.address_label: West Fire Island, Great South Bay — modern island context
rows.why_this_matters: Private subdivision and government conservation are different forms of land control. Neither makes the Native history of this coast disappear, nor establishes that land or authority was returned to a Native nation.

rows.title: West Woods
rows.summary: West Woods is a forty acre beach and woodland area owned by the Shinnecock Tribe. The woodland and beach area is used for contemporary social gatherings, weddings, celebrations, camping, and sweat lodge ceremonies. In recent times, West Woods has been encroached upon with it's blurred boundaries. At the start of the 1747 100-year timber lease to the Shinnecock by Southampton Town, the land encompassed one hundred acres.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added a section on contemporary sweat lodge and coming-of-age ceremonies, with the sweat lodge photograph and associated plant observations and community contributions.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Shinnecock Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Western Southampton: Deeds, Native Objections and Colonial Power
rows.summary: Between Canoe Place and Seatuck, English settlers claimed land through overlapping agreements and a colonial governor’s ruling. Native people retained fishing and gathering rights, demanded continuing payments and challenged who had authority to sell. Westwoods remains Shinnecock land.
rows.address_label: Western Southampton and barrier beaches — modern regional context
rows.why_this_matters: A deed did not silence Native objections or erase every continuing right. Reading the agreements beside the protests and colonial rulings shows who asserted authority, what obligations remained, and why retained Shinnecock land must remain visible in the story.

rows.title: Westhampton Free Library
rows.summary: On This Site by Shinnecock artist Jeremy Dennis will be on view November 1–30, 2026. More exhibition information will be shared soon.
rows.address_label: 7 Library Avenue, Westhampton Beach, NY 11978
rows.why_this_matters: Seeing On This Site at a local library connects contemporary Shinnecock art with places just beyond its doors: Potunk, Apocock and Quantuck. The exhibition offers a starting point for learning whose histories the surrounding landscape holds, and for continuing that exploration after leaving the gallery.

rows.title: Whale's Fin
rows.summary: Whale's Fin is a Shinnecock sacred and cultural place near Shinnecock Inlet, remembered in oral history through whaling, whales coming ashore, and the changing barrier-beach landscape.
rows.address_label: Shinnecock Inlet shoreline area, Southampton (generalized)
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Shinnecock Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
rows.why_this_matters: Whale's Fin connects Shinnecock maritime knowledge with a living cultural landscape. It carries histories of whaling skill, coastal change, and continuing relationships among Shinnecock people, whales, the bay, and the ocean.

rows.title: Whaling
rows.summary: Whaling history on Native Long Island connects whales as living relations, drift-whale harvests, seventeenth-century shore-whaling labor, Shinnecock, Montaukett, and Unkechaug maritime skill, industrial whaling, ecological loss, and present-day whale conservation.
rows.activity_update_summary: Removed an accidentally appended draft maritime article and repeated source tail; retained the complete cited Whaling article and connected Historic Moments.
rows.why_this_matters: Whaling history shows Native Long Island as a maritime homeland shaped by reciprocal relationships with whales, skilled Native labor, colonial exploitation, global travel, and present-day responsibility to living whale populations.

rows.title: Wickapogue (Meacox Bay)
rows.summary: Wickapogue is a farming district at the western end of Meacox Bay in Southampton. The name is interpreted as at the end of the pond or water-place.

rows.title: Wickaposset (Fishers Island)
rows.summary: A small eastern-island place name whose variants preserve older coastal geography beyond the main body of Long Island.

rows.title: Wigwagonock (Sag Harbor)
rows.summary: Wigwagonock is a Sag Harbor placename associated with land east of Division Street and an Indigenous village site near Sleight's Hill.

rows.title: Wigwame Swamp (Cold Spring Harbor)
rows.summary: Wigwame, or Wigwam, is recorded as a swamp in Huntington town. A local note places the early "wigwam swamp" where the main part of Cold Spring Harbor village now stands.

rows.title: William Floyd Estate
rows.summary: In exchange for reconfirming previous land deeds between the Unkechaug and colonist Colonel William Tangier Smith, Smith granted in perpetuity one hundred and seventy-five acres of land to the tribe on Mastic Neck. The grant stated that the Unkechaug, " their children and the posterity of their children forever shall without molestation from me or my heirs or assigns shall and may plant and sowe forever " and added that the Indians could not sell, convey, or alienate this planting right or any part thereof to any.
rows.address_label: 245 Park Dr, Mastic Beach, NY 11951
rows.activity_update_summary: Consolidated the existing dated chronology into cited Historic Moments and removed the duplicate unformatted history block.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Unkechaug Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Winganhauppauge
rows.summary: An Islip brook-and-neck placename sometimes associated with Champlain's Creek, preserving a waterway name before later English naming.
rows.listing_image_alt: Roadside view in the Winganhauppauge landscape. Posted signs mark private property; this photograph does not identify a public entrance. Photograph © Jeremy Dennis, September 12, 2026.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Secatogue Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Winganhauppauge (Champlain's Creek)
rows.summary: Winganhauppauge is an Islip placename tied to a neck of land and brook also associated with Champlain's Creek.
rows.listing_image_alt: Roadside view in the Winganhauppauge landscape. Posted signs mark private property; this photograph does not identify a public entrance. Photograph © Jeremy Dennis, September 12, 2026.

rows.title: Winippague
rows.summary: Winippague is the traditional placename for what is now Bergen Island in Jamaica Bay. The alternative name is Wimbaccoe. Anthropologist William Wallace Tooker suggested that the name may translate to "a fine water-place," from wini, "fine," and -paug, "water-place." Winippague or Bergen Island has been identified as an important wampum manufacturing place for Canarsie people during early contact with Europeans. Archaeological materials from the area are held in Smithsonian collections.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Canarsie Traditional Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Winippague (Bergen Island)
rows.summary: Winippague is recorded for Bergen Island in Jamaica Bay, with Wimbaccoe linked as a related form.

rows.title: Winne-comack / Commack
rows.summary: Winne-comack is associated with modern Commack. Shorter Comac and Comack forms are kept as alternate spellings of the same placename rather than separate map sites.

rows.title: Winnecomac / Commack
rows.summary: Winnecomac is the older placename behind Commack, a hamlet spanning Huntington and Smithtown.

rows.title: Winnecroscoms Neck (Mastic)
rows.summary: Winnecroscoms is a neck of land in Brookhaven town, one of the necks into which Mastic was divided. Related forms include Winocrosscombs, Wenacroscoms, Wenicroscoms, Winecroscum, and Wannuggeashcum.

rows.title: Wisquosucks (Squassucks Point)
rows.summary: Wisquosucks is a Brookhaven placename for Squassucks Point on the Carmans River, associated with an Unkechaug person recorded in deeds and leases.

rows.title: Wonunke (Westhampton)
rows.summary: Wonunke is a Westhampton placename for necks of land east of Beaver Dam River, later appearing in Great and Little Wonunk forms.
rows.address_label: Oneck area, Westhampton Beach, NY (approximate)

rows.title: Wooruskhouse (Probable Copiague Neck)
rows.summary: Rev. Azariah Horton repeatedly mentioned Wooruskhouse in 1741-1743 and located it about three miles from West Neck. The distance, his south-shore travel, the Town of Babylon's historic neck sequence, and the name's possible reference to a point of land make Copiague Neck the strongest modern inference, but not a proven identification.
rows.address_label: Copiague Neck, Town of Babylon, NY (probable broad identification)
rows.why_this_matters: Wooruskhouse records an eighteenth-century Native community landscape along Babylon's south shore. A probable marker restores that name to the map while making the limits of the surviving evidence visible instead of turning Horton's distance note into false certainty.

rows.title: Wopowog (Stony Brook)
rows.summary: Wopowog is recorded for Stony Brook in Brookhaven town, with Wopawog appearing in earlier Long Island history writing.

rows.title: Wuchebehsuck (Montauk North Neck)
rows.summary: A Montauk North Neck valley name associated with a small pond outlet and the 1670 Montauk deed.

rows.title: Wyamaug / Miamogue (Simmons Point)
rows.summary: Wyamaug, also recorded as Miamogue, Miamegg, and Miamuck, is a Jamesport placename associated with Simmons Point.

rows.title: Wyandance / Wyandanch
rows.summary: Wyandance, now Wyandanch, is a Babylon placename preserving the name of the seventeenth-century sachem of Paumanack.

rows.title: Yaphank / Yamphanke
rows.summary: Yaphank is a Brookhaven village name originally applied to a creek south of the hamlet. Yamphanke is an earlier recorded form.

rows.title: Yaphank, Weeks Pond Settlement
rows.summary: Yaphank, a village in Brookhaven town, was originally the name of the creek south of the hamlet. A land deed signed in 1664 by Unkechaug Sachem Tobacus mentions a river called Yamphanke. In the 17th century, the Unkechaug Indians, who had their primary residence in nearby Mastic, built temporary campsites near what was later known as Weeks Pond.
rows.activity_update_summary: Consolidated dated history into the cited Historic Timeline so the listing no longer repeats the same content.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Unkechaug Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.

rows.title: Yennecock / Southold Town
rows.summary: Yennicock and Yennicott are spellings preserved for the North Fork, not simply an old name for today's Southold hamlet. English settlement began in 1640, but the surviving record shows several transactions and later confirming deeds—not one uncontested purchase that transferred the entire Corchaug homeland at once.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added a cited introduction explaining Yennicock's broad North Fork scope, Southold's 1640 settlement, the 1665 confirming deeds, Paucamp's 1660 testimony, and the layered nature of colonial land claims.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Corchaug Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
rows.why_this_matters: Yennicock helps visitors see that a Native place-name could describe a landscape larger than a later town center. Reading the 1640 settlement, repeated deeds, and Paucamp's testimony together prevents the North Fork from being reduced to one colonial founding date. It also keeps Native geographic knowledge, Corchaug authority, and the uneven conversion of homeland into surveyed property visible.

rows.title: Yennicock / Yennicott (Southold)
rows.summary: Yennicock, Yennicott, Yenycott, and related spellings appear in seventeenth-century records for the North Fork. William Wallace Tooker later argued that the name described a broader tract from the Peconic River to Plum Gut, not only the modern Southold village area.
rows.activity_update_summary: Added a source-grounded introduction explaining the recorded Yennicock and Yennicott spelling variants, Tooker's broader North Fork interpretation, and the uncertainty surrounding his proposed translation.
rows.why_this_matters: The variants Yennycok, Yenycott, Yeanocock, and others show how one Indigenous place-name was repeatedly reshaped in colonial spelling. Tooker's wider North Fork interpretation also warns against shrinking an Indigenous geography to the boundaries of a later town. Preserving both the variants and the uncertainty lets visitors see a layered record rather than treating one spelling or marker as final.

rows.title: Yonáhqôsunuk
rows.summary: The Smith Site near Smith Cove preserves evidence of Indigenous use across more than one season as well as an ancestral resting place. Public descriptions remain broad to protect ancestors, cultural belongings, and archaeological deposits.
rows.ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Manhansett Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
rows.why_this_matters: The Smith Cove landscape records enduring Indigenous use of Shelter Island across seasons. It also shows why older archaeological reports must be read critically: ancestors and burial belongings are not objects of curiosity, and precise burial information requires protection.
